title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamically Selecting Draft Model Depth and Feature Fusion Layers Based on Input Complexity
description: Problem: EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion improves draft quality but applies the same architectural configuration uniformly across all inputs, regardless of token predictability. Simple continuations (e.g., boilerplate text) don't require deep feature fusion, while complex reasoning steps do. This static approach wastes compute on easy tokens and may under-invest in hard ones. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a complexity-aware speculative decoding framework built on EAGLE-3. A lightweight router (2-layer MLP trained with a small labeled complexity dataset) estimates per-token prediction difficulty from shallow features before committing to full feature fusion. Based on this estimate, the system dynamically selects (1) how many target model layers to fuse and (2) the draft tree speculation depth. The router is trained jointly with the draft model using a multi-task objective combining acceptance rate prediction and token prediction. Experiments: We evaluate on Llama-3 (8B, 70B) and Qwen-2.5 (7B, 32B) across MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and long-form generation tasks. We measure wall-clock speedup, acceptance rate, and routing overhead. Ablations examine router architectures, fusion layer selection strategies, and performance under varying batch sizes. We hypothesize 10-20% additional speedup over EAGLE-3 on heterogeneous workloads without quality degradation.

title: EAGLE-3 for Multimodal LLMs: Speculative Decoding with Cross-Modal Feature Fusion
description:
Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 have demonstrated impressive speedups for text-only LLMs, but vision-language models (VLMs) such as LLaVA, Qwen-VL, and InternVL remain underexplored in this context. VLMs face unique challenges: the draft model must reason over both visual tokens (from vision encoders) and text tokens simultaneously, and naive application of EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion ignores the heterogeneous nature of these modalities, likely degrading acceptance rates.

Proposed Method: We extend EAGLE-3's training-time test paradigm to VLMs by designing a cross-modal draft model that fuses multi-layer text features (as in EAGLE-3) with compressed visual features extracted from intermediate vision encoder layers. A lightweight cross-attention module aligns visual context with the draft model's token prediction head. We adopt EAGLE-3's direct token prediction objective and scale training data using diverse vision-language corpora (image captioning, VQA, document understanding, chart reasoning).

Experiments: We evaluate on Qwen2-VL-7B and LLaVA-1.6-13B across five tasks: image captioning (COCO), visual QA (MMBench), document QA (DocVQA), multimodal reasoning (MathVista), and open-ended chat. Metrics include speculative decoding speedup ratio, token acceptance rate, and throughput at varying batch sizes. We compare against vanilla speculative sampling, EAGLE-2 adapted for VLMs, and Medusa baselines.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous Speculative Decoding Across Task Distributions
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for general token prediction, but LLM workloads in production are highly heterogeneous—spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, creative writing, and factual QA. A single draft model cannot be simultaneously optimal across all these distributions, leading to suboptimal acceptance rates for out-of-distribution tasks. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, a mixture-of-draft-models framework where multiple lightweight EAGLE-3-style draft models are specialized for distinct task clusters (code, math, chat, retrieval-augmented). At inference time, a lightweight task-type classifier (trained on input embeddings from the first transformer layer) routes each request to the most appropriate draft model. We further introduce a draft-blending mechanism that interpolates token predictions from the top-2 draft models weighted by classifier confidence, gracefully handling ambiguous inputs. To reduce memory overhead, draft models share a common backbone with task-specific adapter heads trained via LoRA. Experiments: We evaluate on diverse benchmarks including HumanEval, MATH-500, MT-Bench, and TriviaQA using Llama-3.1-70B as the target model. We compare speedup ratios, acceptance rates, and memory footprint against EAGLE-3 baseline and per-task fine-tuned drafts, demonstrating that AdaptiveDraft achieves 10-20% higher acceptance rates on specialized tasks with less than 15% additional memory overhead.

title: EAGLE-3 for Multimodal LLMs: Extending Training-Time Test to Vision-Language Speculative Decoding
description: Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 are designed for text-only LLMs, but vision-language models (VLMs) such as LLaVA and Qwen-VL are increasingly deployed in latency-sensitive applications (e.g., real-time visual assistants, medical image analysis). VLMs introduce additional complexity: the draft model must handle heterogeneous input streams (visual tokens from a frozen vision encoder plus text tokens), and the target model's internal features are influenced by cross-modal attention patterns that pure text drafters cannot anticipate. Proposed Method: We extend EAGLE-3's training-time test and multi-layer feature fusion to VLMs by introducing a multimodal-aware draft model that (1) fuses multi-layer text features from the LLM backbone as in EAGLE-3, and (2) incorporates a lightweight cross-attention adapter that conditions the draft on compressed visual context embeddings. During training-time test, we simulate inference conditions by randomly masking subsets of visual tokens, forcing the draft model to be robust to varied visual contexts. The draft model predicts tokens directly rather than features, benefiting from scaled text-image paired training data. Planned Experiments: We evaluate on LLaVA-1.6, InternVL2, and Qwen2-VL across tasks including visual QA, image captioning, OCR, and multi-turn visual dialogue. We measure speedup ratio, acceptance rate, and throughput at varying batch sizes, comparing against vanilla speculative decoding, Medusa, and the text-only EAGLE-3 baseline applied naively to VLMs.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Context-Aware Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding Across Heterogeneous Workloads
description: Problem: Production LLM serving systems handle diverse query types simultaneously — short conversational turns, long reasoning chains, code generation, and retrieval-augmented generation — each with dramatically different token acceptance rate profiles for a fixed draft model. EAGLE-3's single draft model achieves strong average speedup but may be suboptimal for workloads with high distributional variance, leaving throughput gains on the table. Proposed Method: We train a lightweight 'meta-router' that observes the first few tokens of context plus shallow target-model features to select dynamically among a small pool of specialized EAGLE-3 draft models (e.g., one trained predominantly on reasoning traces, one on conversational data, one on code). The meta-router itself is trained via a reward signal derived from empirical acceptance rates on held-out routing decisions, framed as a contextual bandit problem. We additionally propose 'draft model merging' — interpolating weights of specialized drafts at inference time guided by the router's soft assignment — to reduce memory overhead. Experiments: We evaluate on mixed-workload benchmarks combining ShareGPT, HumanEval, MATH reasoning, and RAG tasks, measuring per-category and aggregate tokens-per-second, acceptance rate variance, and memory footprint versus a single EAGLE-3 baseline across batch sizes 1–128 in the SGLang framework.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding Across Heterogeneous Query Distributions
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for a fixed target LLM and task distribution. In production deployments, query distributions shift dramatically across domains (coding, math reasoning, creative writing, chat), causing the draft model's acceptance rate—and thus speedup—to degrade on out-of-distribution inputs. A single static draft model cannot simultaneously excel across all distributions without significant capacity overhead. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a mixture-of-drafts framework that maintains a small pool of lightweight draft heads (2-4), each specialized for a distinct query cluster identified via unsupervised embedding clustering of training data. At inference time, a fast routing classifier (trained jointly via EAGLE-3's training-time test paradigm) selects the most suitable draft head per query based on the input embedding from the target model's middle layers. Each draft head is fine-tuned using EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion and direct token prediction. The router adds negligible latency (<0.5ms). Planned Experiments: (1) Compare acceptance rates and wall-clock speedup across coding (HumanEval), math (MATH-500), creative writing, and chat benchmarks against EAGLE-3 baseline. (2) Ablate number of draft heads (1-6). (3) Evaluate distribution shift robustness with held-out query types. (4) Measure throughput at batch sizes 1-128 in SGLang. Target: 15-25% speedup improvement over EAGLE-3 on mixed-distribution production workloads.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous Speculative Decoding Across Task Types
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 demonstrates strong speedups but uses a single draft model regardless of task type (coding, math reasoning, open-ended chat). Different tasks have fundamentally different token predictability patterns — reasoning chains have high local predictability while creative tasks are more stochastic. A static draft model wastes capacity on easy tokens and underperforms on hard ones, leaving speedup potential unrealized.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight task-type classifier that operates on the first few tokens of each prompt to route requests to task-specialized draft models (e.g., one fine-tuned on reasoning traces, one on code, one on conversational data), all sharing the EAGLE-3 multi-layer feature fusion backbone but with task-specific final layers. We additionally introduce a dynamic draft-depth scheduler that adjusts the speculative lookahead depth (1-6 tokens) based on online acceptance rate statistics per request, allocating more speculation depth to high-acceptance sequences.

Experiments: We evaluate on MT-Bench, HumanEval, MATH, and long-form generation benchmarks using Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 as target models. Metrics include tokens/second, acceptance rate per task category, and draft model switching overhead. Ablations isolate routing vs. dynamic depth scheduling. We compare against vanilla EAGLE-3 and a single-model baseline.

title: SpecFuse: Adaptive Multi-Draft Speculative Decoding via Learned Draft Merging for Diverse Generation Tasks
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 uses a single draft model optimized for one distribution, but LLM inference spans diverse tasks (code, math reasoning, creative writing) with fundamentally different token predictability. A single draft model architecture wastes capacity on easy tokens while failing on hard ones, leaving speedup gains on the table. Proposed Method: We introduce SpecFuse, which trains a small ensemble of lightweight draft heads (2-3 heads, each ~10% of EAGLE-3 cost) specializing in different token distributions, combined with a learned gating network that dynamically selects or merges draft candidates at inference time without target model overhead. The gating uses shallow features from the target model's intermediate layers (available cheaply via multi-layer fusion, inspired by EAGLE-3) to predict which draft head will achieve highest acceptance. During training, we use a multi-task curriculum where each draft head is incentivized to specialize via auxiliary diversity losses. Experiments: We evaluate on code completion (HumanEval), mathematical reasoning (MATH-500), long-form generation (MT-Bench), and structured extraction benchmarks using Llama-3 70B and DeepSeek-R1. Metrics include mean accepted tokens per step, wall-clock speedup, and specialization analysis via token-type acceptance rates. We compare against EAGLE-3 single-head baselines and ablate ensemble size and gating complexity.

title: AdaptDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Inference Workloads
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 demonstrates impressive speedups with a single draft model, but real-world LLM deployments serve heterogeneous workloads—coding, reasoning, chat, summarization—each with different token distributions and acceptance rate profiles. A single draft model trained on mixed data is suboptimal across all task types simultaneously. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptDraft, a routing framework that maintains a small bank of lightweight EAGLE-3-style draft models, each specialized for a distinct task cluster (e.g., reasoning chains, code generation, conversational exchanges). A lightweight task classifier (trained via contrastive learning on prompt embeddings) dynamically selects the appropriate draft model per request at inference time. For multi-turn conversations where task type shifts mid-sequence, we introduce a sliding-window acceptance-rate monitor that triggers draft model switching when acceptance rates fall below a threshold. To avoid overhead from maintaining multiple draft models, we explore low-rank adapter (LoRA) specialization from a shared EAGLE-3 backbone, keeping memory footprint minimal. Experiments: We evaluate on ShareGPT, HumanEval, MATH500, and mixed-workload benchmarks using LLaMA-3 and DeepSeek-R1, measuring token acceptance rates, wall-clock speedup, memory overhead, and throughput at batch sizes 1–64. We compare against a single universal EAGLE-3 draft model and per-task static draft models, demonstrating Pareto improvements in speed-memory tradeoffs across heterogeneous traffic distributions.

title: SpecFusion: Combining Multiple Lightweight Draft Models via Mixture-of-Experts for Adaptive Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a single draft model trained on a fixed data distribution, limiting adaptability across heterogeneous query types (code, math reasoning, chat, etc.). A single draft model must simultaneously handle diverse token distributions, potentially underperforming on specialized domains even with scaled training data.

Proposed Method: We propose SpecFusion, which trains a small mixture-of-experts (MoE) draft model where each expert specializes in a distinct domain (code, math, general conversation, structured output). Using EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion and direct token prediction as the backbone, we add a lightweight router trained jointly with the experts via domain-labeled speculative training data. At inference, the router selects the top-k experts based on fused multi-layer features from the target model, requiring no external domain classifier. We also introduce a domain-aware acceptance criterion that adjusts the speculation temperature per expert.

Experiments: We evaluate on HumanEval, GSM8K, MATH, MT-Bench, and ShareGPT using Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 as target models. Baselines include EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3, and Medusa. Metrics include speedup ratio, acceptance rate per domain, and throughput at varying batch sizes in SGLang, demonstrating that domain-specialized drafting yields superior speedups over single-model approaches.

title: AdaptiDraft: Difficulty-Aware Dynamic Draft Length Scheduling for Speculative Decoding
description: Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed or tree-structured draft budget regardless of token-level generation difficulty. Easy tokens (common phrases, predictable continuations) waste verification budget when over-drafted, while hard tokens (rare terms, complex reasoning steps) suffer from low acceptance rates when under-drafted. This mismatch reduces overall throughput. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiDraft, a lightweight difficulty predictor that operates alongside the EAGLE-3 draft model to dynamically allocate draft length per decoding step. The predictor uses entropy of the draft model's output distribution plus hidden-state uncertainty estimates (via cheap MC-dropout approximation) to classify each step as easy/medium/hard, assigning draft lengths from a discrete set {2,4,8}. The scheduler is trained jointly with the draft model using a reward signal derived from acceptance rate versus compute cost tradeoff. We further introduce a 'confidence-gated early exit' mechanism where the draft model stops generating tokens once predicted acceptance probability falls below a threshold. Experiments: We evaluate on EAGLE-3 backbone (Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, DeepSeek-R1) across MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and long-form generation tasks, measuring tokens/second, acceptance rate distribution, and compute FLOPs. We target demonstrating 10-15% additional throughput gains over EAGLE-3 baseline with no quality degradation.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Aware Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding via Online Routing
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model to approximate a target LLM across diverse tasks. However, a single draft model may be suboptimal across heterogeneous deployment scenarios (code generation, mathematical reasoning, dialogue), where the token distribution and feature dynamics differ substantially. This mismatch reduces acceptance rates and limits speedup gains in specialized domains.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight mixture-of-draft-experts (MoDE) system where multiple small draft heads specialize in distinct domains, guided by a learned online router. The router operates on multi-layer fused features (following EAGLE-3's training-time test paradigm) and dynamically selects or interpolates among draft heads at inference time without querying the target model. Each expert draft head is trained on domain-partitioned data using curriculum learning, while the router is trained jointly via differentiable top-k gating with load balancing.

Planned Experiments: (1) Train MoDE on a mixture of code, math, and chat corpora derived from EAGLE-3's data pipeline. (2) Evaluate acceptance rate and wall-clock speedup on HumanEval, MATH-500, MT-Bench, and long-context summarization against EAGLE-3 and EAGLE-2 baselines. (3) Ablate number of experts (2, 4, 8) and routing granularity (per-token vs. per-sequence). (4) Measure routing overhead and throughput at batch sizes 1–64 in SGLang. We expect 10–20% acceptance rate improvements in specialized domains with negligible routing overhead.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Serving via Workload-Aware Speculative Sampling
description:
Problem: In production LLM serving, requests vary dramatically in nature (coding, reasoning, chat, summarization), yet existing speculative decoding systems like EAGLE-3 use a single fixed draft model regardless of input characteristics. A draft model optimized for chat may perform poorly on mathematical reasoning, leading to low acceptance rates and wasted computation.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight 'meta-router' that analyzes incoming request features (prompt embedding, task type signal, token entropy from prefill) and dynamically selects or blends outputs from a small pool of specialized EAGLE-3 draft models, each trained on domain-specific data (code, math/reasoning, general chat). The router operates with negligible overhead (<1ms) and learns to predict which draft model will achieve the highest token acceptance rate for a given input. We also explore a soft-mixture approach where draft logits from multiple models are weighted by the router's confidence scores.

Experiments: (1) Train 3 specialized EAGLE-3 draft heads for Llama-3.1-70B on domain-specific corpora. (2) Evaluate acceptance rates and end-to-end speedup across MT-Bench, HumanEval, MATH, and summarization benchmarks. (3) Compare against single universal EAGLE-3 draft model. (4) Ablate router architectures and mixture strategies. (5) Test under realistic mixed-workload serving scenarios using SGLang to measure throughput gains at various batch sizes.

title: AdaptEAGLE: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for Speculative Decoding via Continual Learning
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3's draft model is trained on general-purpose data, yielding strong average performance but suboptimal speedups in specialized deployment domains (e.g., medical reasoning, legal drafting, code generation in niche languages) where target model distributions diverge significantly from training data. A domain-specific draft model could dramatically improve acceptance rates, but retraining from scratch per domain is prohibitively expensive.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptEAGLE, a continual learning framework that efficiently specializes EAGLE-3 draft models to target domains without catastrophic forgetting. Starting from a pretrained EAGLE-3 draft model, we apply parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA adapters) on domain-specific corpora while using elastic weight consolidation (EWC) regularization to preserve general-domain acceptance rates. We further introduce a 'draft temperature scaling' mechanism that dynamically adjusts draft model confidence based on detected domain shift at inference time.

Experiments: (1) Train domain adapters for 5 domains: medical QA, legal text, scientific papers, code, and mathematical reasoning. (2) Measure speedup ratios and token acceptance rates versus base EAGLE-3 across domains. (3) Ablate EWC vs. LoRA vs. combined approaches. (4) Evaluate catastrophic forgetting on MT-Bench after domain adaptation. (5) Compare compute cost of adapter fine-tuning vs. full retraining. We expect 15-25% acceptance rate improvements in specialized domains with minimal general-domain degradation.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Aware Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding via Lightweight Query Routing
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model on large mixed datasets, but real-world LLM deployments serve heterogeneous queries spanning code, math reasoning, creative writing, and dialogue. A single draft model may under-specialize, leaving acceptance rate gains on the table for specific domains even after data scaling. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, a routing framework that maintains a small pool of domain-specialized EAGLE-3 draft models (e.g., code, math, general) alongside a lightweight query router (a small MLP or embedding similarity classifier operating on the first 32 tokens). At inference time, the router selects the most appropriate draft model with negligible overhead (<1ms). During training, we partition EAGLE-3 training data by domain clusters (using automated topic classifiers) and fine-tune specialized draft heads from a shared backbone, preserving the multi-layer feature fusion of EAGLE-3. A mixture-of-drafts variant additionally combines token proposals from two draft models via weighted voting when the router is uncertain. Experiments: We evaluate on domain-specific benchmarks (HumanEval, MATH-500, MT-Bench, LongBench) using Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 targets, measuring acceptance rate, wall-clock speedup, and router overhead. We compare against single EAGLE-3, per-domain EAGLE-3, and random routing baselines, targeting 10-20% additional speedup over EAGLE-3 on specialized domains.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding Across Heterogeneous Query Distributions
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for a fixed data distribution, but real-world LLM deployments face highly heterogeneous query distributions (code, math, chat, reasoning) where a single draft model may excel on some tasks while underperforming on others. Serving systems that route diverse queries to one draft model leave significant speedup potential unrealized. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight query-routing framework that maintains a small ensemble of specialized EAGLE-3 draft models (e.g., one each for code, math/reasoning, and general chat), each trained on domain-specific data using the training-time test technique. At inference time, a fast query classifier (fine-tuned embedding model, <10M parameters) routes each request to the most suitable draft model. We additionally propose a draft model merging strategy using task vectors to reduce memory overhead while preserving specialization. Experiments: (1) We benchmark acceptance rates and wall-clock speedup across five domains (HumanEval, MATH, MT-Bench, ShareGPT, scientific QA) comparing single universal draft vs. AdaptiveDraft ensemble vs. merged variants. (2) We analyze classifier latency overhead vs. speedup gains under varying batch compositions. (3) We evaluate memory-accuracy tradeoffs of merged draft models. Target models: Llama-3.1-8B/70B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Serving via Workload-Aware Speculative Sampling
description:
Problem: In production LLM serving, requests vary dramatically in task type (coding, reasoning, chat, math), and a single draft model trained with EAGLE-3's multi-layer fusion approach may not optimally accelerate all workload types. The acceptance rate of draft tokens depends heavily on input distribution alignment between draft and target models, yet current speculative decoding systems use a fixed draft model regardless of incoming query characteristics.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, a routing framework that maintains a small pool of specialized EAGLE-3 draft models (e.g., one fine-tuned on reasoning traces, one on code, one on conversational data) and learns a lightweight workload classifier that predicts which draft model maximizes expected token acceptance rate for a given input. The classifier uses the first few tokens and a brief prefix-embedding to route requests. We further introduce a draft model blending mechanism that interpolates logits from two draft models when classification confidence is low, using the multi-layer features from EAGLE-3 as a common representation backbone.

Experiments: We evaluate on Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen-2.5-72B across MT-Bench, HumanEval, MATH-500, and mixed production traces. Metrics include per-category speedup ratios, acceptance rates, and end-to-end throughput under realistic heterogeneous batch serving scenarios, compared against single-draft EAGLE-3 and Oracle draft selection baselines.

title: AdaptDraft: Input-Adaptive Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 and similar speculative decoding methods use a single fixed draft model regardless of input characteristics. However, different query types (mathematical reasoning, code generation, open-ended chat) have fundamentally different token predictability patterns, suggesting that a single draft architecture is suboptimal across all domains. A lightweight draft model may suffice for simple queries while complex reasoning chains demand a more capable drafter.

Proposed Method: We train a small routing network that observes the input prompt and initial target model hidden states to dynamically select from a pool of draft models of varying capacity (e.g., 1-layer, 3-layer, and 6-layer EAGLE-3 style draft heads). The router is trained jointly with the draft pool using a multi-objective loss balancing acceptance rate against draft model FLOPs. At inference, the router adds negligible overhead while steering queries to the most compute-efficient draft model.

Planned Experiments: (1) Train draft model pools on Llama-3.1-70B and DeepSeek-R1 using EAGLE-3's training-time test paradigm. (2) Evaluate adaptive routing vs. single-model baselines on MT-Bench, HumanEval, MATH, and long-document summarization. (3) Measure wall-clock speedup, acceptance rate per domain, and router overhead. (4) Ablate pool size and routing granularity (per-prompt vs. per-token routing).

title: AdaptiDraft: Difficulty-Aware Dynamic Draft Length Selection for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed or tree-based draft budget regardless of token-level generation difficulty. Easy tokens (e.g., function words, predictable continuations) waste compute on large draft trees, while hard tokens (rare entities, complex reasoning steps) may benefit from deeper speculation. This mismatch limits throughput gains, especially in heterogeneous workloads mixing easy and hard generation contexts.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiDraft, a difficulty-aware controller that dynamically adjusts draft length and tree width at inference time. Using lightweight signals from EAGLE-3's multi-layer fused features—specifically the entropy of the draft model's token distribution and acceptance rate history—we train a small online policy (a 2-layer MLP) to predict optimal draft budget per decoding step. The controller is trained via a lightweight RL objective maximizing tokens-per-second subject to a target acceptance rate constraint, using rollout data collected during standard inference.

Experiments: We evaluate on MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and long-document summarization tasks using Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 as target models. Baselines include EAGLE-3 with fixed tree configurations and SpecTr. Metrics include wall-clock speedup, acceptance rate, and throughput at varying batch sizes (1, 16, 64). We hypothesize AdaptiDraft achieves 10-20% additional speedup over EAGLE-3 by reducing wasted speculation on easy tokens.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Task-Aware Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding via Online Routing
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 demonstrates that a single draft model trained on diverse data can achieve strong average speedups, but different tasks (coding, math reasoning, open-ended chat, RAG) exhibit fundamentally different token distribution patterns. A single monolithic draft model must compromise across these regimes, leaving task-specific speedup potential untapped. Proposed Method: We train a small family of lightweight, specialized draft models (one per task cluster) using EAGLE-3's training-time test framework, then learn a cheap routing network that observes the prompt context and recent draft acceptance rates to dynamically select or interpolate between draft models at inference time. The router is trained via a bandit-style online learning objective that maximizes expected token acceptance rate as a proxy reward, without requiring task labels at test time. We also explore merging draft model weights via task vectors to reduce memory overhead while retaining specialization benefits. Experiments: We evaluate on EAGLE-3's five benchmark tasks plus additional domains (SQL generation, scientific QA) using Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 as target models. Metrics include per-task speedup ratio, acceptance rate, and wall-clock throughput at batch sizes 1–64 in SGLang. We compare against EAGLE-3's single draft model, showing that adaptive routing yields 10–25% additional speedup on specialized tasks with minimal memory overhead.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Online Difficulty-Aware Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous Speculative Decoding
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model to accelerate a fixed target LLM, but real-world inference involves highly variable query complexity—simple factual queries require few speculative steps while complex multi-step reasoning demands longer, more accurate drafts. A one-size-fits-all draft model wastes compute on easy queries and underperforms on hard ones. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a framework that maintains a bank of draft models with varying capacity (small/medium/large) trained using EAGLE-3's training-time test paradigm, and dynamically selects which draft model to deploy per-query at inference time. A lightweight routing network, trained online via bandit feedback (acceptance rate signals), predicts query difficulty from the first few target-model hidden states and selects the appropriate draft model before speculative rollout begins. The router is updated continuously using contextual bandit updates, requiring no labeled difficulty annotations. Planned Experiments: (1) Train 3 draft model variants per target LLM (Llama-3-8B, Qwen-2.5-32B) using EAGLE-3's approach. (2) Evaluate on mixed-difficulty benchmarks: MT-Bench, GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval, and long-form summarization. (3) Compare throughput, acceptance rate, and latency against single best-draft EAGLE-3 baseline. (4) Ablate router architectures and online update frequency. We expect 15-25% additional throughput gains on heterogeneous workloads.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Input-Complexity-Aware Dynamic Draft Length Scheduling for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed or heuristically-tuned draft length (number of speculative tokens generated per step), ignoring that different input prompts and generation contexts have vastly different acceptance rate profiles. Easy continuations (e.g., repetitive text, code boilerplate) can tolerate longer drafts, while complex reasoning steps require shorter, more careful drafts. This mismatch wastes compute or leaves speedup potential unrealized.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight 'draft length predictor' — a small MLP head attached to EAGLE-3's multi-layer fused features — that predicts the optimal draft length (from a discrete set, e.g., 3–12 tokens) before each drafting step. The predictor is trained via reinforcement learning using acceptance rate as the reward signal, optimizing wall-clock latency rather than a static proxy. We incorporate a simple online calibration mechanism that adapts the predictor at inference time using a running statistics buffer of recent acceptance rates per context type.

Experiments: (1) Speedup benchmarks on MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and long-form generation tasks against EAGLE-3 with fixed draft lengths; (2) Ablation on predictor architecture and RL reward shaping; (3) Throughput scaling analysis across batch sizes 1–128 in SGLang; (4) Analysis of predicted draft lengths vs. task complexity to validate interpretability.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Serving via Workload-Aware Speculative Sampling
description:
Problem: In production LLM serving, request workloads are heterogeneous—coding tasks, reasoning chains, and casual chat exhibit vastly different token acceptance rate profiles under speculative decoding. A single static draft model (even EAGLE-3) leaves significant speedup on the table because it cannot adapt to query-type-specific token distributions at runtime.

Proposed Method: We train a small family of lightweight EAGLE-3-style draft models, each specialized on a distinct domain (code, math/reasoning, general chat). We introduce a fast workload classifier that runs on the first few prompt tokens (~1ms overhead) to route each request to the most suitable draft model. For ambiguous or mixed requests, we propose a mixture-of-drafts mechanism that dynamically blends token proposals from two candidates weighted by online acceptance rate feedback within the same batch. A continual fine-tuning procedure using EAGLE-3's training-time test framework keeps each specialist current as base models are updated.

Planned Experiments: (1) Acceptance rate and wall-clock speedup across domain-stratified benchmarks (HumanEval, MATH, MT-Bench, ShareGPT) comparing single EAGLE-3 vs. AdaptiveDraft. (2) Throughput under mixed-workload batching in SGLang at batch sizes 1–128. (3) Ablation of routing accuracy impact on end-to-end speedup. (4) Cost of maintaining specialist pool vs. speedup gain trade-off analysis.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for EAGLE-3 via Continual Meta-Learning
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model on general-purpose data, but real-world LLM deployments are often domain-specific (e.g., medical, legal, code generation). A general draft model may mispredict tokens in specialized vocabularies and syntax patterns, reducing acceptance rates and speedup in deployment. Training separate draft models per domain is expensive and inflexible when domains shift at inference time.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, which treats domain adaptation of EAGLE-3 draft models as a meta-learning problem. Using MAML-style meta-training across diverse domain corpora, we train a draft model with an initialization that rapidly adapts to new domains with few gradient steps using only unlabeled target-domain text (via self-supervised token acceptance signal from the frozen target LLM). At inference time, a lightweight online adapter (LoRA, ~1M params) is continuously updated using recent token acceptance/rejection signals as a reward, enabling the draft model to track distribution shifts without interrupting serving.

Experiments: (1) Measure acceptance rate and wall-clock speedup on domain-specific benchmarks: PubMedQA, LegalBench, HumanEval, and financial QA. (2) Compare against EAGLE-3 baseline, domain-specific fine-tuned drafts, and vanilla continual learning. (3) Evaluate adaptation speed (steps to peak acceptance rate) and throughput under streaming domain-shift scenarios. (4) Ablate meta-learning vs. online LoRA adaptation contributions independently.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Adaptive Speculative Decoding via Lightweight Draft Model Fine-Tuning with Multi-Layer Feature Fusion
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 demonstrates that multi-layer feature fusion with direct token prediction significantly improves speculative decoding. However, a single draft model trained on general data may underperform when the target LLM is deployed in specialized domains (medical, legal, code generation), as the token distribution shifts substantially from general pretraining data. Repeatedly retraining the full draft model for each domain is prohibitively expensive. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, which maintains a lightweight domain adapter (low-rank LoRA modules) on top of EAGLE-3's draft model architecture. Using a small unlabeled corpus from the target domain (~10K examples), we apply parameter-efficient fine-tuning using EAGLE-3's training-time test objective while freezing the base draft model weights. The multi-layer feature fusion heads are updated alongside the LoRA adapters, allowing rapid domain specialization (<1 GPU-hour). A mixture-of-adapters mechanism enables multi-domain serving by routing based on prompt embeddings. Planned Experiments: (1) Compare acceptance rates and speedup ratios across medical (MedQA), legal (LegalBench), and code (HumanEval) domains against vanilla EAGLE-3 and domain-specific baselines. (2) Ablate LoRA rank, number of training examples, and which feature fusion layers to adapt. (3) Evaluate adapter switching overhead and throughput in multi-domain serving scenarios with SGLang at varying batch sizes.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Task-Aware Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 demonstrates that a single draft model can achieve impressive speedups, but different inference tasks (code generation, math reasoning, open-ended chat, summarization) exhibit vastly different token distribution patterns and acceptance rates. A static draft model is suboptimal across this diversity — a draft model trained on reasoning traces may underperform on creative writing and vice versa. Proposed Method: We train a small family of lightweight EAGLE-3-style draft models, each specialized on a different task distribution (coding, reasoning, instruction-following, factual QA). At inference time, we introduce a lightweight task classifier operating on the first few prompt tokens to route each request to the most suitable draft model. We further propose a 'draft ensemble fallback' mechanism: when the classifier confidence is low, we blend token probabilities from two draft heads to handle ambiguous mixed-task inputs. All draft heads share a common backbone initialized from EAGLE-3 multi-layer fusion, with task-specific fine-tuning heads added on top to minimize additional memory. Experiments: We evaluate on MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, MATH-500, and TruthfulQA using Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5, measuring speedup ratio, acceptance rate, and classifier overhead. We compare against a single EAGLE-3 draft model and task-specific fine-tuned baselines, showing 10-20% additional speedup on task-homogeneous workloads with negligible routing latency.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for EAGLE-3 via Continual Learning
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3's draft model is trained on general data and achieves strong average speedups, but domain-specific inference tasks (e.g., medical reasoning, code generation, legal analysis) exhibit highly skewed token distributions that cause draft acceptance rates to drop significantly compared to general benchmarks. A single static draft model cannot optimally serve all deployment domains.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight continual learning framework that fine-tunes EAGLE-3's draft model on domain-specific unlabeled data using only target model forward passes as supervision signals (no human labels). Leveraging EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion architecture, we selectively fine-tune a small set of domain adaptation layers (LoRA-style) while freezing the base draft model, preventing catastrophic forgetting across domains. We further introduce a domain-mixture replay buffer to maintain general performance. At deployment, a lightweight domain classifier automatically selects the appropriate adapter.

Experiments: (1) Speedup ratio comparisons across 6 specialized domains (medical QA, legal text, code, math, scientific papers, multilingual) vs. baseline EAGLE-3; (2) Acceptance rate analysis pre/post adaptation; (3) Continual learning benchmarks measuring forgetting on general tasks; (4) Ablation on LoRA rank, replay buffer size, and number of adaptation layers; (5) Overhead analysis of domain classifier and adapter switching latency at various batch sizes.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding Across Heterogeneous Query Distributions
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for average-case performance, but real-world LLM deployments encounter highly heterogeneous query distributions (code, math reasoning, casual chat, long-form generation). A single draft model may achieve high acceptance rates on some query types while performing poorly on others, leaving significant speedup potential unrealized.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a mixture-of-drafts framework that maintains a small pool of specialized lightweight draft models (2-4 models), each trained via EAGLE-3's training-time test paradigm on domain-specific data. At inference time, a fast query classifier (trained jointly) routes incoming requests to the most appropriate draft model. We further propose a confidence-weighted blending mechanism that softly interpolates draft token distributions when queries span multiple domains. To avoid router overhead, the classifier operates on the first few tokens of KV-cache features already computed by the target model.

Experiments: (1) Train specialized drafts for code (HumanEval/MBPP), math (MATH/GSM8K), reasoning (AIME), and chat (MT-Bench) domains using Llama-3-8B and Qwen-2.5-72B as targets. (2) Evaluate speedup ratio, token acceptance rate, and routing accuracy across mixed-distribution benchmarks. (3) Ablate number of draft models, router architectures, and blending strategies. (4) Measure latency overhead of routing vs. speedup gains at various batch sizes in SGLang.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for Speculative Decoding via Continual Training-Time Test
description: Problem: EAGLE-3's training-time test technique dramatically improves draft model quality for general-purpose LLMs, but specialized deployment domains (medical, legal, code generation) exhibit significant distributional shift from pretraining data. A single draft model trained on general corpora may produce poor token acceptance rates when the target model is fine-tuned or prompted for specialized domains, negating speedup gains. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, which extends EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion and direct token prediction with a lightweight continual adaptation mechanism. Specifically, we (1) maintain a small domain-specific replay buffer populated during inference, (2) periodically fine-tune only low-rank adapter (LoRA) modules in the draft model using training-time test on domain samples without modifying the target model, and (3) employ an acceptance-rate-aware learning rate scheduler that intensifies adaptation when observed token acceptance falls below a threshold. This allows the draft model to continuously track domain shift with minimal overhead. Planned Experiments: We evaluate on four specialized domains (medical QA, legal documents, Python code, mathematical reasoning) using domain-fine-tuned Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 target models. Metrics include speedup ratio, token acceptance rate, adaptation wall-clock overhead, and quality preservation (ROUGE, pass@k). Baselines include EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3 without adaptation, and full draft model retraining.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Serving Workloads
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for a specific target LLM and general task distribution. In production serving, workloads are highly heterogeneous—mixing code generation, reasoning chains, casual chat, and factual QA—each with distinct token distributions and optimal speculation depths. A static draft model leaves significant speedup on the table for specialized request types.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight routing and specialization framework built on EAGLE-3. First, we train a small set of task-specialized EAGLE-3 draft models (e.g., code, reasoning, chat) using domain-filtered data, exploiting EAGLE-3's demonstrated data-scaling capability. Second, we train a ultra-lightweight request classifier (<1M params) that predicts the optimal draft model given the first few tokens of a prompt. Third, we introduce a mid-generation switching mechanism that monitors acceptance rate statistics online and can hot-swap draft models when the distribution shifts (e.g., a reasoning chain transitioning to code output).

Experiments: Evaluate on mixed-workload benchmarks combining HumanEval, MATH, MT-Bench, and TriviaQA with realistic traffic distributions. Compare mean speedup, P95 latency, and throughput against single EAGLE-3 draft, EAGLE-2, and vanilla speculative decoding. Ablate routing accuracy, switching overhead, and the impact of draft model count on performance-efficiency tradeoffs.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Serving via Workload-Aware Speculative Sampling
description:
Problem: Production LLM serving faces highly heterogeneous workloads—coding queries, reasoning chains, casual chat—each with distinct token distribution patterns. A single fixed draft model (as in EAGLE-3) may be suboptimal across this diversity, leaving significant acceleration potential untapped. Different tasks benefit from draft models trained on task-specific data, but switching models adds overhead and complexity.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, a serving framework that maintains a small pool of lightweight EAGLE-3-style draft models, each specialized for a task cluster (e.g., code, math reasoning, general chat). At inference time, a ultra-lightweight query classifier (distilled from the target LLM's first two layers) routes each request to the most appropriate draft model. We further introduce a 'draft blending' mechanism that interpolates token predictions from multiple draft models weighted by classifier confidence, avoiding hard routing failures. Draft models share a common multi-layer feature fusion backbone fine-tuned from a single base draft, with task-specific heads—minimizing memory overhead.

Experiments: We evaluate on ShareGPT, HumanEval, MATH, and mixed-workload benchmarks using Llama-3.1-70B and DeepSeek-R1. Metrics include speedup ratio, acceptance rate per task type, GPU memory overhead, and routing latency. We compare against single-draft EAGLE-3, SpecInfer, and oracle per-task routing baselines.

title: EAGLE-3 for Long-Context Reasoning: Adaptive Draft Length Scheduling via Speculative Chain-of-Thought
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 demonstrates strong speedups for standard chat and reasoning tasks, but long-context reasoning (e.g., multi-step mathematical proofs, multi-hop QA over long documents) presents a distinct challenge: token acceptance rates vary dramatically across reasoning phases (problem setup vs. computation vs. conclusion), making a fixed draft length suboptimal and potentially degrading throughput. Proposed Method: We introduce Adaptive Speculative Scheduling (AdaSS), which augments EAGLE-3's draft model with a lightweight phase classifier that predicts the current reasoning stage from multi-layer fused features. Based on predicted phase, AdaSS dynamically adjusts the draft length at each speculation step—shorter drafts during high-entropy exploratory reasoning phases and longer drafts during deterministic conclusion phases. We additionally propose a phase-aware training objective that fine-tunes the EAGLE-3 draft model on long-context reasoning traces, explicitly teaching it to model intra-trace distributional shifts. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) MATH-500 long-solution split, (2) LongBench multi-hop QA, (3) AIME 2024/2025 with extended chain-of-thought, and (4) coding tasks with long context windows. Metrics include wall-clock speedup, token acceptance rate by reasoning phase, and task accuracy. We compare against fixed-length EAGLE-3, EAGLE-2, and Medusa baselines.

title: AdaptDraft: Dynamically Selecting Draft Model Complexity Based on Input Difficulty for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 achieves impressive speedups with a fixed draft model architecture, but not all inputs require the same drafting capability. Simple, repetitive, or formulaic prompts (e.g., code boilerplate, factual lookups) could be served by a shallower, faster draft model, while complex reasoning chains demand the full multi-layer feature fusion of EAGLE-3. A static draft model wastes capacity on easy inputs and may underperform on hard ones.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight 'difficulty router' that predicts, from the prompt and partial generation context, which of K draft model variants (ranging from a tiny 1-layer MLP to the full EAGLE-3 architecture) should be invoked for the next drafting step. The router is trained end-to-end using acceptance rate as a proxy reward signal via a differentiable surrogate, with draft model variants sharing a backbone but differing in depth and feature fusion layers. At inference, the router dynamically switches draft models per decoding step.

Experiments: We evaluate on MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and long-context summarization tasks using Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 targets. Metrics include wall-clock speedup, acceptance rate, router overhead, and speedup decomposed by prompt difficulty quintile. Baselines include EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3, and a static ensemble. We hypothesize 10-20% additional speedup over EAGLE-3 on mixed-difficulty workloads.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Serving via Workload-Aware Speculative Sampling
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for a specific target LLM, but production serving environments handle diverse workloads—coding, reasoning, chat, math—with vastly different token distribution characteristics. A monolithic draft model cannot optimally accelerate all query types, leaving significant speedup potential unrealized.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a framework that maintains a small pool of lightweight, specialized draft models (each fine-tuned on domain-specific corpora using EAGLE-3's training-time test and multi-layer feature fusion). At inference time, a ultra-lightweight workload classifier (trained on prompt embeddings) routes each request to the most suitable draft model. We further propose a 'draft blending' mechanism that dynamically interpolates token predictions from multiple draft models when classification confidence is low, weighted by per-domain acceptance rate estimates computed online.

Experiments: (1) Train 4 specialized EAGLE-3 draft models for Llama-3.1-70B covering coding (HumanEval/MBPP), math (MATH dataset), reasoning (ARC/HellaSwag), and chat (ShareGPT). (2) Compare against single universal EAGLE-3 draft on mixed workload benchmarks measuring speedup ratio, acceptance rate, and classifier overhead. (3) Ablate routing strategies (hard routing vs. soft blending) and pool sizes. (4) Evaluate throughput under realistic batch serving with heterogeneous request streams in vLLM/SGLang.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding Across Heterogeneous Query Distributions
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for a fixed target LLM, but real-world serving involves heterogeneous query distributions (coding, reasoning, chat, math) where a single draft model may have highly variable acceptance rates across domains, leaving performance on the table. A draft model trained on balanced data may be suboptimal for specialized workloads.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a mixture-of-draft-experts framework where multiple lightweight domain-specialized draft heads (sharing the EAGLE-3 multi-layer feature fusion backbone) are trained via domain-conditional routing. At inference time, a lightweight query classifier (trained jointly via distillation) selects or interpolates among draft heads. We further propose an online adaptation mechanism: using sliding-window acceptance rate statistics per request batch to dynamically reweight draft head contributions without retraining.

Experiments: (1) Train domain-specialized draft heads on Llama-3-8B/70B using coding (HumanEval, SWE-bench), math (MATH, GSM8K), and chat (MT-Bench, ShareGPT) corpora. (2) Evaluate speedup ratios vs. EAGLE-3 single-head baseline across domain-specific and mixed workloads. (3) Ablate routing strategies (hard vs. soft, online vs. static). (4) Measure throughput in SGLang under realistic mixed traffic. Expected: 10-20% additional speedup on specialized workloads with minimal overhead from routing.

title: AdaptDraft: Domain-Adaptive Speculative Decoding via Lightweight Draft Model Fine-Tuning with Multi-Layer Feature Fusion
description: Problem: EAGLE-3's draft model is trained on general-purpose data, but LLMs are frequently deployed in specialized domains (medical, legal, code generation) where token distributions differ significantly from general training data. A general draft model may exhibit poor acceptance rates in these domains, negating speedup gains. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptDraft, which leverages EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion architecture as a foundation for rapid domain adaptation. Given a target LLM fine-tuned for a specific domain, we develop a parameter-efficient adaptation protocol where only lightweight LoRA adapters (< 5M parameters) are trained on top of the frozen EAGLE-3 draft model using domain-specific data. Crucially, we introduce a domain-aware feature routing mechanism that learns to weight contributions from different target model layers differently per domain, without modifying the frozen target model. We additionally propose a consistency regularization loss that prevents catastrophic forgetting of general-domain acceptance rates during domain fine-tuning. Experiments: We evaluate on medical QA (MedQA), legal reasoning (LegalBench), scientific literature (S2ORC), and code synthesis (HumanEval) using Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 as target models. Metrics include token acceptance rate, wall-clock speedup, and adaptation cost (GPU-hours). We compare against full EAGLE-3 retraining, vanilla LoRA fine-tuning, and no-adaptation baselines.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous Speculative Decoding Across Task Domains
description: Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 train a single draft model to approximate a fixed target LLM across all task types. However, different tasks (code generation, mathematical reasoning, open-ended chat) exhibit fundamentally different token distribution dynamics, causing a universal draft model to be suboptimal—either over-spending capacity on simple tasks or under-performing on complex ones. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight task-routing framework that maintains a small pool of specialized EAGLE-3-style draft models, each fine-tuned on domain-specific corpora (code, math reasoning chains, conversational text). At inference time, a ultra-lightweight classifier (trained on the first few tokens of context) selects the most suitable draft model before speculative decoding begins. We additionally propose a draft model merging technique inspired by model merging literature to compress the pool into a single multi-head draft model with task-conditioned gating, eliminating routing overhead. Experiments: We evaluate on HumanEval, MATH-500, MT-Bench, and a mixed-domain benchmark using Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 as target models. Metrics include acceptance rate per domain, wall-clock speedup, and throughput at various batch sizes. We compare against single universal EAGLE-3 draft models and demonstrate that domain-specialized routing improves average acceptance rate by ~8-15% with negligible routing overhead.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Confidence-Aware Dynamic Draft Length Scheduling for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed or heuristically-tuned draft length at inference time, ignoring that token predictability varies substantially across query types, contexts, and model confidence levels. This mismatch causes wasted computation on difficult tokens where drafts are frequently rejected, and missed speedup opportunities on easy tokens where longer drafts would be accepted.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight meta-controller that dynamically adjusts draft length per decoding step. The controller uses three signals: (1) the draft model's token-level confidence distribution entropy, (2) a rolling acceptance rate estimate over recent steps, and (3) query-type embeddings from a small classifier distinguishing factual, reasoning, and creative tasks. These signals feed a small MLP trained via reinforcement learning with a reward balancing tokens-per-second against acceptance rate. We integrate AdaptiveDraft with EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion, replacing its static tree-attention with confidence-gated variable-depth drafts.

Experiments: We evaluate on MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and long-form generation benchmarks using Llama-3-8B/70B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill. We measure speedup ratios, acceptance rates, and throughput at batch sizes 1–128. Ablations isolate contributions of each signal. We hypothesize 10-20% additional speedup over EAGLE-3 on heterogeneous workloads where query difficulty varies.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Input-Complexity-Aware Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed draft model regardless of input complexity, causing inefficiency — simple queries waste capacity on a powerful draft model while complex reasoning queries suffer from a weak one. A one-size-fits-all draft model leaves significant latency and accuracy gains on the table.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight routing classifier that operates on target model intermediate features (similar to EAGLE-3's multi-layer fusion) to predict query complexity at inference time and dynamically select from a pool of 2-3 draft models of varying sizes (e.g., 0.5B, 1B, 3B). The router is trained jointly with the draft models using a multi-objective loss balancing acceptance rate prediction and routing overhead. We also introduce a speculative confidence score that triggers mid-sequence draft-model switching when complexity shifts within a generation (e.g., a coding question spawning a mathematical proof).

Experiments: (1) Compare against fixed EAGLE-3 on MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and MATH across Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 families. (2) Measure wall-clock speedup, acceptance rates, and routing overhead. (3) Ablate static vs. dynamic mid-sequence switching. (4) Analyze routing decisions qualitatively across task types. We expect 15-25% additional throughput improvement over EAGLE-3 on mixed-complexity workloads.

title: AdaptEAGLE: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for Speculative Decoding via Continual Training-Time Test
description: Problem: EAGLE-3's training-time test technique demonstrates that multi-layer feature fusion with scaled data significantly improves draft model quality. However, a single universal draft model trained on general corpora may perform suboptimally in specialized deployment domains (e.g., medical reasoning, code generation, legal documents) where token distributions diverge substantially from general training data, leaving acceptance rates and speedup ratios well below their potential. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptEAGLE, a lightweight domain adaptation framework for EAGLE-3 draft models. Rather than retraining the full draft model, we introduce domain-specific low-rank adapters (LoRA) inserted into the draft model's multi-layer feature fusion module, trained on small domain-specific corpora (~100M tokens) using the training-time test objective from EAGLE-3. We additionally propose a domain mixture inference strategy that dynamically selects or interpolates between adapters based on input context embeddings, enabling a single deployed system to handle multiple domains efficiently. Experiments: We evaluate on four specialized domains—biomedical QA (MedQA), competitive programming (LiveCodeBench), legal reasoning (LegalBench), and mathematical proofs (Lean4 corpora)—comparing against EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3 (no adaptation), and full fine-tuning baselines. Metrics include token acceptance rate, wall-clock speedup, and adapter training cost. We target demonstrating 15-25% acceptance rate improvement over domain-agnostic EAGLE-3 with under 2 GPU-hours of adaptation per domain.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for Speculative Decoding via Continual Meta-Learning
description:
Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 train a single draft model intended to generalize across diverse tasks (coding, reasoning, chat). However, token distribution shifts dramatically across domains, and a one-size-fits-all draft model incurs suboptimal acceptance rates in specialized deployment scenarios (e.g., a production coding assistant or medical reasoning system). Rapidly adapting draft models to target domains without full retraining remains unsolved.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, which frames draft model specialization as a continual meta-learning problem. Starting from an EAGLE-3 draft model, we apply a reptile-style meta-learning outer loop during training across diverse domain corpora, so the draft model learns parameter initializations that quickly adapt to new domains. At deployment, given a small unlabeled in-domain prompt corpus (~100 examples), we perform efficient few-shot fine-tuning (LoRA, ~minutes on one GPU) to produce a domain-specialized draft model. We introduce a domain-shift detection module that monitors draft acceptance rates online and triggers re-adaptation when distribution drift is detected.

Experiments: We evaluate on four deployment scenarios: medical QA, legal reasoning, code generation, and scientific literature. Metrics include token acceptance rate, end-to-end speedup ratio, and adaptation compute cost. We compare against vanilla EAGLE-3, task-specific EAGLE-3 fine-tuning from scratch, and standard LoRA fine-tuning without meta-initialization, demonstrating that AdaptiveDraft achieves competitive domain-specific speedups with 10x less adaptation data and compute.

title: SpecFusion: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for EAGLE-3 via Continual Learning from Deployment Feedback
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3's draft model is trained once and deployed statically, but real-world LLM usage exhibits strong domain shifts (e.g., code generation vs. mathematical reasoning vs. conversational chat). A draft model optimized on general data may have poor acceptance rates in specialized deployment contexts, negating the speedup gains.

Proposed Method: We propose SpecFusion, a continual learning framework that adapts EAGLE-3's draft model online during deployment. As the target LLM processes requests, we collect (accepted token, rejected token) pairs from the speculative sampling verification step as free supervision signal—no additional labeling needed. We use this signal to fine-tune the draft model via a lightweight LoRA adapter using elastic weight consolidation (EWC) to prevent catastrophic forgetting across domains. An automatic domain detector clusters incoming prompts and maintains separate LoRA adapters per domain, routing at inference time.

Planned Experiments: (1) Measure acceptance rate and wall-clock speedup across domain shifts: general→code, general→math, general→legal on Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1. (2) Compare against static EAGLE-3 and periodic full retraining baselines. (3) Ablate EWC vs. naive fine-tuning to quantify forgetting. (4) Evaluate adaptation speed: speedup improvement as a function of number of deployment samples. (5) Measure overhead of online LoRA updates on throughput at batch sizes 1, 16, 64.

title: AdaptDraft: Domain-Adaptive Draft Model Fine-Tuning for Speculative Decoding via Lightweight LoRA Fusion
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single universal draft model that approximates the target LLM's token distribution across all domains. However, specialized deployment scenarios (e.g., medical reasoning, code generation, legal document drafting) have highly skewed token distributions that a general-purpose draft model poorly approximates, reducing speculative decoding acceptance rates precisely where consistent latency matters most.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptDraft, a framework for rapidly adapting EAGLE-3-style draft models to target domains using lightweight LoRA fine-tuning with only ~1-5K domain-specific examples. We introduce a domain-aware multi-layer feature fusion module that learns to weight contributions from different target model layers differently per domain, combined with a speculative-acceptance-rate-maximizing training objective (rather than standard cross-entropy) that directly optimizes the draft acceptance probability under the target model's distribution. A small router network selects domain-specific LoRA adapters at inference time with negligible overhead.

Experiments: (1) Acceptance rate and speedup across specialized domains (medical QA, competitive coding, legal reasoning) vs. general EAGLE-3 baseline. (2) Ablation of LoRA rank, number of training samples, and layer fusion weighting. (3) Throughput evaluation in SGLang with adapter switching overhead. (4) Transfer efficiency: few-shot adaptation curves comparing AdaptDraft against full draft model retraining. We target >15% acceptance rate improvement over vanilla EAGLE-3 on specialized benchmarks with <2 GPU-hours of adaptation.

title: AdaptDraft: Dynamically Selecting Draft Model Depth Based on Input Complexity for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 uses a fixed draft model architecture regardless of input complexity—simple queries waste compute on deep multi-layer fusion while hard reasoning queries may benefit from deeper drafting. There is no mechanism to match draft model capacity to per-input difficulty, leaving efficiency gains on the table.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptDraft, a complexity-aware speculative decoding framework built on EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion backbone. We train a lightweight router (a small MLP taking compressed hidden states as input) that predicts, at inference time, how many fusion layers and draft tokens to generate per decoding step. The router is trained jointly with the draft model using a combined objective: token prediction loss plus a regularization term penalizing unnecessary compute. During inference, the router dynamically selects from a discrete set of draft configurations (e.g., 1-layer fast path, 3-layer standard path, 5-layer deep path) and adjusts the speculation length per step.

Experiments: (1) Measure acceptance rate and wall-clock speedup across complexity-stratified benchmarks (GSM8K, HumanEval, MT-Bench, long-context QA). (2) Ablate router architectures and routing granularities. (3) Compare against fixed-depth EAGLE-3 baselines at matched average FLOPs budgets. (4) Analyze routing decisions to validate that harder inputs trigger deeper drafting. Target: 10-15% additional speedup over EAGLE-3 at equivalent quality.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Task-Aware Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding via Online Meta-Learning
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for general token prediction, but LLM inference workloads are highly heterogeneous—code generation, mathematical reasoning, and conversational tasks exhibit fundamentally different next-token distributions. A single draft model must compromise across these distributions, leaving task-specific acceptance rates suboptimal. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, a framework that maintains a small pool of lightweight draft models (each fine-tuned on domain-specific corpora using EAGLE-3's training-time test technique) and a meta-routing module that dynamically selects or interpolates between draft models at inference time. The router is a tiny MLP taking as input the multi-layer fused features from EAGLE-3 plus a short context embedding, trained via online meta-learning (MAML-inspired) to maximize token acceptance rate as a proxy reward. We further introduce a mixture-of-drafts decoding mode where draft trees are assembled by sampling candidate tokens from multiple domain drafts proportionally to router confidence scores. Experiments: We evaluate on coding (HumanEval), math reasoning (MATH-500), long-form generation (MT-Bench), and retrieval-augmented QA tasks using Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 targets. Metrics include acceptance rate, end-to-end speedup, and routing overhead. We compare against EAGLE-3 single-model baseline and SpecInfer, targeting 15-25% additional speedup on domain-specific workloads with negligible routing latency overhead.

title: AdaptEAGLE: Domain-Adaptive Draft Model Fine-Tuning for Speculative Decoding in Specialized LLM Deployments
description: Problem: EAGLE-3's draft model is trained on general-purpose data, yielding strong average speedups but suboptimal acceptance rates when the target LLM is deployed in narrow specialized domains (e.g., biomedical reasoning, legal text, code generation). Domain shift between general training data and inference-time token distributions reduces draft acceptance rates, limiting practical speedup gains in production deployments. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptEAGLE, a lightweight continual fine-tuning framework for EAGLE-3 draft models that adapts them to a target domain with minimal compute. Specifically, we (1) collect a small domain corpus (~50K examples), (2) apply parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) to the EAGLE-3 draft model using EAGLE-3's training-time test objective on domain data while freezing the target LLM, and (3) introduce a domain-mixing regularization loss to prevent catastrophic forgetting of general-purpose drafting ability, controlled by a KL-divergence penalty against the original draft model's token predictions. Experiments: We evaluate on four specialized domains—biomedical QA (MedQA), legal reasoning (LegalBench), mathematical proofs (MATH), and code completion (HumanEval)—measuring token acceptance rate, wall-clock speedup, and perplexity of accepted sequences. Baselines include vanilla EAGLE-3 and full retraining. We target Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 as backbone models.

title: AdaptDraft: Input-Adaptive Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous Speculative Decoding
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 achieves impressive speedups using a single draft model trained with multi-layer feature fusion, but different input types (code, math reasoning, chat, creative writing) exhibit vastly different token predictability and acceptance rate profiles. A one-size-fits-all draft model leaves significant performance on the table for specialized domains. Proposed Method: We train a small portfolio of lightweight EAGLE-3-style draft models, each specialized on a distinct data distribution (code, chain-of-thought reasoning, conversational, factual QA). At inference time, a micro-classifier (a tiny MLP operating on the first few target model hidden states after the prompt prefix) routes each request to the most suitable draft model. The router is trained jointly with the draft models using a multi-task objective combining acceptance rate maximization and routing confidence. We also explore dynamic switching mid-generation when the content type shifts (e.g., a reasoning model transitioning from natural language analysis to symbolic computation). Experiments: We evaluate on diverse benchmarks including HumanEval, MATH, MT-Bench, TriviaQA, and long-form generation tasks. Metrics include per-domain acceptance rates, wall-clock speedup, and routing overhead. Ablations compare single universal draft vs. routed portfolio, and static vs. dynamic mid-generation routing, demonstrating that domain-specialized drafts with learned routing yield 15-25% additional speedup over a single EAGLE-3 draft model.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Input-Complexity-Aware Dynamic Draft Length Scheduling for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed or heuristically-tuned draft length regardless of input complexity. Easy queries (factual lookups, short completions) waste compute generating long draft sequences with poor acceptance rates, while complex reasoning queries (math, code) could benefit from longer drafts when the draft model is confident. This mismatch limits overall throughput gains.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight meta-controller trained on top of EAGLE-3's draft model that dynamically predicts optimal draft length per forward pass. The controller observes: (1) draft token probability distributions (entropy as uncertainty signal), (2) input prompt embeddings compressed via a small MLP, and (3) historical acceptance rates from recent tokens in the same sequence. Using these signals, it outputs a draft-length decision from a discrete set {1,2,...,K}. We train the controller via reinforcement learning with a reward function balancing token acceptance rate and wall-clock latency, using EAGLE-3 as the frozen base.

Experiments: We evaluate on MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, MATH, and long-form generation benchmarks. Metrics include speedup ratio, acceptance rate, and throughput at varying batch sizes. Ablations test each signal's contribution. We compare against EAGLE-3 with fixed draft lengths and existing dynamic speculative decoding baselines across Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 model families.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamically Selecting Draft Model Architecture and Depth Based on Input Complexity for Speculative Decoding
description: Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed draft model architecture regardless of input complexity. Simple queries waste compute on an over-capable draft model, while complex reasoning chains may benefit from deeper draft models — a static approach misses this opportunity for further speedup gains. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, which trains a lightweight 'routing network' that analyzes the current context (token entropy, query type classifier, reasoning depth signal from chain-of-thought indicators) and dynamically selects from a small pool of draft model variants differing in depth (1-layer, 2-layer, 3-layer) and feature fusion strategy. The routing network is trained jointly with the draft models using reinforcement learning, where reward combines acceptance rate and actual wall-clock latency improvement. For simple factual queries, a shallow 1-layer draft is selected; for multi-step reasoning, deeper drafts with richer feature fusion (borrowing from EAGLE-3's multi-layer fusion) are activated. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) mixed-complexity benchmarks including MT-Bench, HumanEval, and GSM8K with Llama-3.1 and Qwen-2.5 models, (2) measuring per-query latency distributions, (3) ablations comparing fixed vs. adaptive selection, and (4) throughput at varying batch sizes in SGLang. We expect 10-20% additional speedup over EAGLE-3 on mixed workloads.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Serving via Workload-Aware Speculative Sampling
description:
Problem: In production LLM serving, requests span dramatically different task types (coding, reasoning, chat, translation), yet current speculative sampling systems like EAGLE-3 deploy a single draft model regardless of incoming workload characteristics. A draft model trained on one distribution may have poor acceptance rates on out-of-distribution tasks, wasting compute on rejected tokens.

Proposed Method: We train a small pool of lightweight EAGLE-3-style draft models, each specialized for a distinct task cluster (reasoning-heavy, creative/chat, structured output, multilingual). We then train a fast workload classifier operating on the first 32 tokens of each request to route it to the appropriate draft model. Additionally, we introduce a confidence-based fallback: if draft acceptance rate drops below a threshold mid-generation (indicating distribution shift), the system dynamically switches draft models without restarting generation.

Experiments: (1) Acceptance rate and wall-clock speedup across 8 task benchmarks (GSM8K, HumanEval, MT-Bench, WMT, etc.) comparing single-draft EAGLE-3 vs. AdaptiveDraft. (2) Ablation on classifier overhead vs. speedup gains. (3) Batch serving throughput on mixed-workload traces simulating real production traffic distributions. (4) Analysis of mid-generation draft switching frequency and its impact on latency. Target model: Llama-3-70B and DeepSeek-R1.

title: AdaptDraft: Task-Aware Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Workloads
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for general text generation, but real-world LLM deployments serve heterogeneous workloads—coding, reasoning, conversation, retrieval-augmented generation—each with distinct token distributions and acceptance rate profiles. A one-size-fits-all draft model leaves significant speedup gains on the table.
