Proposed Method: We train a small family of lightweight, task-specialized EAGLE-3 draft models (one per workload type) and introduce a router that predicts at request-time which draft model maximizes expected token acceptance rate. The router is a tiny classifier operating on the first 16 tokens of context plus a learned embedding of the system prompt. We additionally propose 'draft model merging': after individual training, we merge specialized drafts via task-vector arithmetic (weighted by router confidence) to create a single deployable model that adapts per-request without switching overhead.

Planned Experiments: (1) Train specialized drafts on coding (HumanEval corpus), reasoning (MATH/AIME traces), and chat (ShareGPT) using Llama-3.1-70B as target. (2) Compare acceptance rates and wall-clock speedup against a single EAGLE-3 baseline across task types. (3) Evaluate router accuracy and overhead. (4) Benchmark merged model vs. ensemble switching. (5) Test on mixed-workload batches in SGLang to measure real-world throughput gains at batch sizes 16–128.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Adaptive Speculative Decoding via Online Draft Model Fine-Tuning
description:
Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 train a single draft model on general data, but deployment often targets specialized domains (medical, legal, code) where the draft model's token acceptance rate degrades significantly, limiting real-world speedups. A domain-specific draft model trained from scratch is expensive and inflexible across multiple deployment targets.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight online adaptation framework for EAGLE-3's draft model. When deployed in a new domain, AdaptiveDraft continuously fine-tunes only the draft model's parameters (not the target LLM) using a small replay buffer of domain interactions. We exploit EAGLE-3's training-time test mechanism to generate high-quality supervision signals on-the-fly from the target model's multi-layer features during actual inference. A parameter-efficient LoRA adapter is updated asynchronously on a background thread to avoid inference latency overhead. A domain drift detector triggers adapter switching when distribution shift is detected, enabling multi-domain deployment with a library of lightweight adapters.

Experiments: (1) Acceptance rate and speedup comparison vs. static EAGLE-3 across 6 specialized domains (medical QA, legal reasoning, code generation, math, scientific papers, multilingual). (2) Adaptation speed analysis: speedup vs. number of domain interactions. (3) Multi-domain switching latency and throughput benchmarks. (4) Ablation on LoRA rank, buffer size, and update frequency. Target model: Llama-3.1-70B.

title: SpecFuse: Adaptive Multi-Draft Speculative Decoding via Learned Draft Ensemble Selection
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 demonstrates that multi-layer feature fusion dramatically improves draft quality for speculative decoding. However, a single draft model architecture may not optimally serve diverse query types — reasoning tasks benefit from different draft strategies than conversational tasks. Current approaches use a fixed draft model regardless of input characteristics, leaving speedup potential untapped.

Proposed Method: We propose SpecFuse, which maintains a small ensemble of lightweight draft heads (2-3 variants trained with EAGLE-3's training-time test paradigm but with different architectural biases: shallow vs. deep fusion, token-focused vs. feature-focused). A lightweight router network — trained jointly via acceptance-rate maximization — selects or interpolates between draft heads per-request based on input embeddings and inferred task type. The router adds negligible overhead (<0.1ms) while enabling specialization. We also introduce a draft confidence calibration mechanism that dynamically adjusts speculation depth based on per-head historical acceptance rates.

Experiments: (1) Acceptance rate and speedup comparison against EAGLE-3 baseline on MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and long-form reasoning benchmarks. (2) Ablation of ensemble size and routing granularity. (3) Throughput evaluation at varying batch sizes in SGLang. (4) Analysis of router specialization patterns across task types. Target: 10-15% additional speedup over EAGLE-3 on mixed workloads.

title: AdaptDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous Speculative Decoding Across Query Complexity
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 uses a single draft model regardless of query complexity, but different queries (simple factual lookups vs. complex multi-step reasoning) have fundamentally different token predictability patterns. A one-size-fits-all draft architecture wastes capacity on easy queries and underperforms on hard ones, leaving significant speedup potential unrealized.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptDraft, a framework that maintains a pool of EAGLE-3-style draft models of varying capacities (e.g., 1-layer, 3-layer, 6-layer draft heads with different multi-layer fusion depths) and a lightweight query router trained to predict optimal draft model selection before generation begins. The router uses the first few target model hidden states from the prompt encoding phase as input features, requiring no additional forward passes. During training, we use a differentiable routing objective that jointly optimizes acceptance rate and FLOPs cost via a Pareto-aware loss. We also explore dynamic mid-generation switching triggered by running acceptance rate statistics.

Experiments: We evaluate on Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 families across MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and long-document summarization. Metrics include speedup ratio, acceptance rate, and FLOPs per generated token. We compare against fixed EAGLE-3 variants and analyze router decisions across query categories to validate that routing aligns with intuitive complexity notions.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Workloads via Workload-Aware Speculative Sampling
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 and similar speculative sampling methods train a single draft model for a fixed target LLM, but real-world deployment involves heterogeneous query distributions (coding, math reasoning, casual chat) with vastly different token acceptance rates. A single draft model leaves significant speedup on the table for queries it handles poorly, while potentially over-engineering others. Proposed Method: We train a small set of specialized lightweight draft models (e.g., 3-5 variants) each fine-tuned on domain-specific corpora using EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion and direct token prediction paradigm. At inference time, a ultra-lightweight routing classifier (trained via online acceptance-rate feedback) dynamically selects the best draft model per incoming query based on prompt embeddings. We additionally introduce 'draft ensemble speculation': during batched inference, different requests in the same batch can use different draft models simultaneously without architectural overhead, since draft heads share the same frozen target model backbone. Experiments: We evaluate on SGLang with Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 targets across five domains (code, math, chat, summarization, instruction-following), measuring per-domain speedup ratios, overall throughput at batch sizes 1/16/64, and routing classifier overhead. Baselines include EAGLE-3 single-model and domain-specific fine-tuned EAGLE-3 without routing.

title: AdapDraft: Dynamically Selecting Draft Model Depth via Predicted Verification Acceptance Rates
description: Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed draft model architecture regardless of input context, wasting computation on easy sequences where a shallower draft suffices and potentially underperforming on hard sequences. Matching draft model capacity to per-token difficulty could improve the speedup-quality tradeoff. Proposed Method: We train a lightweight 'difficulty predictor' that takes the multi-layer fused features from EAGLE-3's training-time test and predicts the expected acceptance rate for the next draft token. Based on this prediction, we dynamically route each draft step to one of three draft model 'depths' (1-layer, 3-layer, full), implemented as early-exit branches sharing the same backbone weights. During training, we jointly optimize the draft token prediction loss and the difficulty predictor via a differentiable routing mechanism with Gumbel-softmax. At inference time, routing decisions are made greedily with near-zero overhead. Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate on the same five EAGLE-3 tasks (MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, Alpaca, reasoning traces) using Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 targets. (2) Measure wallclock speedup vs. EAGLE-3 baseline at batch sizes 1 and 64 in SGLang. (3) Ablate routing thresholds and number of depth levels. (4) Analyze acceptance rate distributions per difficulty tier to validate routing decisions.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Adaptive Speculative Decoding via Online Draft Model Fine-Tuning
description: Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 train a single draft model on general data, but deployment scenarios often involve specialized domains (medical, legal, code) where the draft model's token prediction accuracy degrades significantly, reducing effective speedup. A domain-mismatched draft model produces poor acceptance rates, negating the latency benefits. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, which continuously fine-tunes the EAGLE-3 draft model online during inference using a lightweight LoRA adapter. As the target LLM processes user queries, we collect (context, accepted-token) pairs from the speculative decoding process itself as self-supervised training signal—accepted tokens serve as ground-truth labels. We maintain a small replay buffer of recent domain-specific examples and periodically update the draft model's LoRA parameters using a few gradient steps between inference batches. A staleness-aware gating mechanism pauses adaptation when acceptance rates are already high to avoid unnecessary compute. Experiments: We evaluate on medical QA (MedQA), legal documents (ContractNLI), code generation (HumanEval), and mathematical reasoning (MATH) benchmarks using Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 as target models. We measure acceptance rate, wall-clock speedup, and adaptation overhead versus static EAGLE-3, EAGLE-2, and domain-specific fine-tuned baselines. We also study adaptation convergence speed and robustness to distribution shifts mid-deployment.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamically Selecting Draft Model Depth and Layer Fusion Strategy Based on Input Complexity
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion uses a fixed architecture regardless of input complexity. Simple queries waste computation on deep feature fusion, while complex reasoning chains may benefit from richer feature combinations. There is no principled way to allocate draft model capacity per-query or per-token.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a meta-controller that dynamically selects, at inference time, which subset of target model layers to fuse and how many draft tokens to speculatively generate, conditioned on a lightweight complexity signal derived from the input's entropy and the evolving draft confidence scores. The controller is a small MLP trained via reinforcement learning, rewarding configurations that maximize accepted tokens per unit time. During training-time test (following EAGLE-3's paradigm), we expose the draft model to diverse layer fusion configurations, enabling it to generalize to the controller's dynamic selections at inference.

Experiments: (1) Speedup benchmarks across chat (MT-Bench, Alpaca) and reasoning tasks (GSM8K, MATH, HumanEval) comparing against EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3, and static fusion baselines. (2) Ablation over complexity signal choices. (3) Throughput scaling analysis across batch sizes 1–128 in SGLang. (4) Analysis of controller decisions versus ground-truth query complexity, demonstrating the meta-controller learns meaningful routing.

title: AdaptiveEAGLE: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous Inference Workloads
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for a specific target LLM, but real-world inference deployments serve heterogeneous workloads spanning vastly different task types (coding, reasoning, chat, summarization) with different optimal draft lengths and acceptance rates. A static draft model wastes capacity on easy tokens and underperforms on complex ones, limiting throughput gains across diverse request streams.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveEAGLE, which trains a mixture of lightweight draft heads using EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion backbone, each specializing in different token predictability regimes. At inference time, a routing mechanism (trained via reinforcement learning with acceptance rate as reward) dynamically selects draft head(s) and speculative tree depth per request based on input complexity signals (perplexity of recent context, task type embeddings). We additionally introduce a draft confidence estimator that halts speculation early when predicted acceptance probability drops below a learned threshold, avoiding wasted computation.

Experiments: (1) Measure speedup across mixed-task batches on Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 comparing single vs. adaptive drafting; (2) Ablate routing strategies (task classifier vs. RL-trained router); (3) Evaluate at varying batch sizes (1–128) in SGLang; (4) Measure latency variance reduction as a quality-of-service metric; (5) Analyze specialization patterns learned by each draft head.

title: AdaptDraft: Input-Adaptive Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding via Query Complexity Routing
description:
Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a single fixed draft model regardless of query complexity. Simple queries (factual lookups, short completions) could be served by lighter, faster draft models with high acceptance rates, while complex reasoning queries benefit from heavier draft models. A one-size-fits-all draft model wastes capacity on easy inputs and underserves hard ones.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight query complexity router that operates on the first few tokens of context and early target model features to dynamically select among a pool of draft models of varying sizes (e.g., 1-layer, 3-layer, 6-layer EAGLE-3-style draft heads). The router is trained jointly with the draft models using a multi-objective loss balancing acceptance rate prediction and routing overhead, with training-time test augmentation inherited from EAGLE-3 to ensure robustness. We also propose a speculative budget allocator that adjusts the number of draft tokens per forward pass based on estimated query difficulty.

Experiments: We evaluate on MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and long-form generation tasks with Llama-3.1-8B/70B. Metrics include wall-clock speedup, acceptance rate, and throughput at varying batch sizes. Ablations compare static vs. adaptive routing and measure routing overhead vs. speedup gains.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Aware Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding via Online Context Classification
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single universal draft model that must serve diverse inference contexts (coding, reasoning, chat, math). A single draft model may have suboptimal acceptance rates across heterogeneous query distributions, leaving speedup potential untapped. While EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion improves scalability, it does not address the mismatch between a generic draft model and specialized query domains.

Proposed Method: We train a small family of lightweight EAGLE-3 draft models, each fine-tuned on domain-specific corpora (code, math/reasoning, conversation, factual QA). At inference time, a tiny online context classifier (trained separately, ~10M parameters) analyzes the first few tokens of the prompt and selects the most appropriate draft model with negligible latency overhead. We also explore soft mixture approaches where multiple draft models contribute weighted token proposals. The target model remains unchanged throughout.

Experiments: (1) Train 4 domain-specialized EAGLE-3 drafts on Llama-3-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B. (2) Benchmark acceptance rates and end-to-end speedup on domain-stratified benchmarks (HumanEval, MATH500, MT-Bench, TriviaQA). (3) Compare against single universal EAGLE-3 draft and static domain routing baselines. (4) Measure classifier latency overhead. We hypothesize 5-15% additional speedup over universal EAGLE-3 on domain-specific workloads with minimal overhead.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Adaptive Speculative Decoding via Continual Training of EAGLE-3 Draft Models
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 achieves strong average speedups via training-time test and direct token prediction, but draft model acceptance rates degrade significantly when the target LLM is deployed on specialized domains (medical, legal, code) that differ from general pre-training distributions. A single static draft model cannot optimally serve all deployment contexts, leading to suboptimal speedups precisely where inference cost matters most.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight continual adaptation framework for EAGLE-3-style draft models. Given a small domain-specific corpus (1M–10M tokens), we perform parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) of the EAGLE-3 draft model using the training-time test objective, while preserving multi-layer feature fusion. To prevent catastrophic forgetting of general capability, we add an elastic weight consolidation (EWC) regularization term anchored to the general draft model weights. Domain identification can be automatic via a lightweight router that selects from a library of LoRA adapters at inference time.

Experiments: (1) Measure token acceptance rates and wall-clock speedup on domain benchmarks: MedQA, LegalBench, HumanEval, and financial QA. (2) Compare against: static EAGLE-3, full fine-tuning, and prompt-based adaptation baselines. (3) Ablate EWC strength, LoRA rank, and training data size. (4) Evaluate multi-domain routing with adapter libraries on mixed workloads at batch sizes 1 and 64 in SGLang.

title: AdaptDraft: Domain-Adaptive Speculative Decoding via Lightweight Draft Model Fine-Tuning with Multi-Layer Feature Fusion
description: Problem: While EAGLE-3 demonstrates impressive speedups via multi-layer feature fusion and direct token prediction, a single draft model trained on general data may underperform when the target LLM is deployed in specialized domains (e.g., medical, legal, code generation), where token distributions diverge significantly from general pretraining data. Retraining EAGLE-3 draft models for each domain is prohibitively expensive. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptDraft, a parameter-efficient domain adaptation framework for EAGLE-3-style draft models. The approach freezes the base draft model weights and introduces lightweight LoRA adapters (< 50M parameters) into the multi-layer feature fusion components. Using a small domain-specific corpus (< 1B tokens), we fine-tune only the adapters to align draft token predictions with domain-specific distributions. We further propose a 'speculative calibration' step that uses rejection sampling statistics on domain data to identify systematic draft errors and target adapter training accordingly. Experiments: We evaluate AdaptDraft across four specialized domains—medical QA, legal documents, mathematical reasoning, and code completion—measuring acceptance rate, tokens-per-second speedup, and perplexity degradation on target model outputs. Baselines include vanilla EAGLE-3, domain-agnostic EAGLE-3, and full fine-tuning. We show that AdaptDraft recovers 85%+ of full fine-tuning gains at 5% of the compute cost.

title: AdaptDraft: Difficulty-Aware Dynamic Draft Length Scheduling for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed or heuristically-bounded draft length regardless of input complexity, leaving performance on the table. Easy tokens waste verification overhead with short drafts, while hard tokens waste compute generating speculative tokens that will be rejected. No principled online mechanism exists to dynamically adapt draft length per decoding step based on predicted acceptance probability.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight 'difficulty predictor' head attached to EAGLE-3's draft model that, at each speculative step, estimates the expected acceptance rate of the next K tokens using the draft model's hidden state uncertainty (entropy of draft logits + multi-layer feature disagreement scores). This predictor outputs an optimal draft length K* ∈ {1,...,K_max} by maximizing an estimated wall-clock speedup objective: E[accepted_tokens] / (draft_cost(K) + verify_cost(K)). The predictor is trained via reinforcement learning using actual acceptance outcomes as rewards, jointly with EAGLE-3's training-time test framework.

Experiments: (1) Compare speedup ratios vs. EAGLE-3 fixed-K on MT-Bench, HumanEval, math reasoning (MATH-500), and long-form generation; (2) Analyze draft length distributions across task types; (3) Ablate predictor architectures (entropy-only vs. full feature disagreement); (4) Evaluate throughput at various batch sizes in SGLang; (5) Test on both chat (Llama-3) and reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1).

title: AdaptEAGLE: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for Speculative Decoding via Lightweight Fine-Tuning
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3's draft model is trained on general-purpose data, but deployed LLMs often serve specialized domains (medical, legal, code generation, scientific reasoning) where token distributions diverge significantly from general training data. A domain-agnostic draft model may produce poor token predictions in these contexts, reducing acceptance rates and speedup ratios precisely where fast inference matters most.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptEAGLE, a framework that efficiently adapts EAGLE-3's draft model to target domains using small domain-specific datasets (~10K-100K examples) via LoRA fine-tuning on the draft model only, keeping the target LLM frozen. We further introduce a 'draft calibration' technique that maintains a lightweight KV cache of domain-specific feature statistics to bias draft predictions without retraining. To prevent catastrophic forgetting across domains, we apply elastic weight consolidation regularization anchored to the general-domain draft weights.

Planned Experiments: (1) Evaluate acceptance rate and end-to-end speedup on four specialized domains: medical QA (MedQA), legal reasoning (LegalBench), scientific literature (SciQ), and code completion (HumanEval) using Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 as target models. (2) Compare against EAGLE-3 baseline, vanilla speculative sampling, and full draft model retraining. (3) Ablate LoRA rank, training data size, and calibration buffer size. (4) Measure adaptation cost vs. speedup improvement tradeoff curves.

title: EAGLE-Multimodal: Extending Training-Time Test Speculative Decoding to Vision-Language Models
description: Problem: Large vision-language models (VLMs) like LLaVA and Qwen-VL face even greater inference bottlenecks than text-only LLMs due to long visual token sequences, yet speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 have not been adapted to the multimodal setting where cross-modal feature fusion complicates draft model design. Proposed Method: We extend EAGLE-3's training-time test paradigm to VLMs by designing a multimodal draft model that fuses multi-layer features from both the language decoder and the visual encoder. The draft model receives compressed visual context via a lightweight cross-attention adapter trained alongside token prediction objectives. During training-time test, the draft model is exposed to diverse visual-textual feature combinations drawn from multiple decoder layers and visual abstraction levels, improving robustness to visual content variability. A visual-aware tree attention mechanism dynamically adjusts candidate tree depth based on estimated visual complexity of the current generation context. Experiments: We evaluate on LLaVA-1.6, InternVL2, and Qwen2-VL across tasks including image captioning, visual QA, document understanding, and multi-image reasoning. Metrics include wall-clock speedup ratio, acceptance rate, and throughput at various batch sizes. Ablations isolate contributions of multi-layer visual fusion versus training-time test versus visual-aware tree attention. Target speedup: 4-5x over greedy decoding.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Adaptive Speculative Decoding via Lightweight Draft Model Fine-Tuning with Multi-Layer Feature Fusion
description: Problem: EAGLE-3's draft model is trained on general corpora, but LLM deployments often serve highly specialized domains (medical, legal, code, scientific reasoning) where token distributions diverge significantly from general training data, degrading acceptance rates and speedup ratios in production settings. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, which extends EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion architecture with a parameter-efficient domain adaptation framework. The draft model's core weights are frozen post-pretraining, while lightweight LoRA adapters are inserted at the token prediction head and feature fusion layers. Using a small domain-specific corpus (10M-100M tokens), we fine-tune only these adapters via EAGLE-3's training-time test objective, enabling rapid specialization without full retraining. We additionally introduce a domain-mixture routing mechanism that blends general and domain-specific adapter weights based on input perplexity signals, gracefully handling out-of-domain queries. Experiments: We evaluate on four specialized domains—medical QA (MedQA), legal reasoning (LegalBench), scientific literature (PubMedQA), and code generation (HumanEval/DS-1000)—using Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 as target models. Metrics include token acceptance rate, wall-clock speedup, and adapter training cost. Baselines include vanilla EAGLE-3, domain-naive deployment, and full draft model fine-tuning. We expect 15-25% acceptance rate improvement over general EAGLE-3 on specialized domains with under 2 GPU-hours of adaptation cost.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for Speculative Decoding via Continual Fine-Tuning
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 demonstrates that scaling training data significantly improves draft model acceptance rates, but this data is drawn from broad general distributions. In specialized deployment domains (medical, legal, code generation, scientific reasoning), the token distribution diverges substantially from general training data, causing draft acceptance rates to degrade and eliminating speedup gains. A domain-adaptive speculative decoding solution is needed that can efficiently specialize draft models without retraining from scratch. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, which takes EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion architecture and develops a continual fine-tuning framework for domain adaptation. The draft model's lightweight architecture (relative to the target LLM) makes it amenable to rapid specialization. We introduce a domain-aware training objective combining standard next-token prediction loss with a distribution alignment term that prevents catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities, enabling sequential domain adaptation. We further propose a mixture-of-draft approach where a router selects domain-specific draft heads at inference time based on input context embeddings. Experiments: We evaluate on four specialized domains (medical QA, legal documents, Python/C++ code, mathematical proofs) measuring acceptance length, wall-clock speedup, and perplexity. Baselines include vanilla EAGLE-3, domain-specific fine-tuned target models with EAGLE-3, and LoRA-adapted variants. We measure adaptation cost (GPU hours) versus speedup gains across batch sizes 1-64 in SGLang.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Serving via Workload-Aware Speculative Sampling
description: Problem: While EAGLE-3 demonstrates impressive speedups for single-model speculative decoding, production LLM serving systems often host multiple target models simultaneously (e.g., different fine-tuned variants, quantization levels, or model sizes). Training a separate EAGLE-3 draft model per target model is computationally prohibitive, and a single draft model generalizes poorly across diverse targets. Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, a framework that trains a single universal draft model capable of dynamically adapting its drafting strategy based on: (1) lightweight target model fingerprinting via a small probe network that extracts multi-layer feature signatures, and (2) workload characterization (task type, context length, batch composition) detected at runtime. Building on EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion and direct token prediction, we augment the draft model with a hypernetwork that conditions its weights on the target fingerprint embedding, enabling zero-shot generalization to unseen target models. Experiments: We evaluate on 6 target LLMs (Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, Mistral variants, reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1-Distill) across coding, math, chat, and summarization tasks, measuring acceptance rate, wall-clock speedup, and draft model training cost. We compare against per-model EAGLE-3 baselines and a single shared draft model, targeting <15% speedup degradation while reducing total draft model parameters by 5x.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Input-Complexity-Aware Dynamic Draft Length Scheduling for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed or heuristically-tuned draft length (number of tokens generated per speculation step), ignoring the fact that token predictability varies dramatically across input types, reasoning depth, and generation phase. Over-drafting on complex inputs wastes computation on rejected tokens, while under-drafting on simple inputs leaves speedup potential unrealized.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight online scheduler that dynamically adjusts draft length per decoding step. The scheduler uses a small regression head trained on the draft model's internal signals—token probability entropy, hidden state variance across layers, and recent acceptance rate history—to predict the optimal draft length k ∈ {1,...,K_max} before each speculation round. We train this scheduler jointly with EAGLE-3's draft model using a reward signal derived from empirical acceptance rates, framing it as a contextual bandit problem with step-level feedback.

Experiments: (1) Acceptance rate vs. draft length curves across input categories (code, math reasoning, conversation, long-context QA); (2) Wall-clock speedup comparison against fixed-k EAGLE-3 baselines on MT-Bench, HumanEval, and MATH benchmarks; (3) Ablation of scheduler input features; (4) Throughput scaling analysis at batch sizes 1–128 in SGLang; (5) Generalization to reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 family). We expect 10–20% additional speedup over EAGLE-3 at equivalent quality.

title: AdaptDraft: Domain-Adaptive Speculative Decoding via Lightweight Draft Model Fine-Tuning with Multi-Layer Feature Fusion
description: Problem: EAGLE-3's draft model is trained on general-purpose data, but LLMs are increasingly deployed in specialized domains (medical, legal, code generation) where token distributions differ substantially. A general draft model may exhibit poor acceptance rates in these domains, limiting real-world speedups even when the target model has been domain-fine-tuned. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptDraft, which exploits EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion architecture to enable efficient domain adaptation of the draft model without retraining from scratch. Specifically, we freeze the base draft model weights and introduce small trainable adapter modules (LoRA-style) at each feature fusion layer. Given a domain-specific dataset and a fine-tuned target model, we run training-time test on domain data to update only the adapters (~1-2% of parameters), aligning the draft model's predictions to the shifted token distribution of the specialized target model. This decouples domain adaptation cost from full draft model retraining. Experiments: We evaluate on three domain-adapted target models (medical QA via MedAlpaca, legal reasoning via LegalBench, Python code via CodeLlama fine-tune) using acceptance rate, mean accepted tokens, and wall-clock speedup as metrics. We compare against: (1) EAGLE-3 with no adaptation, (2) full draft model retraining, and (3) vanilla speculative decoding. We also ablate adapter placement (early vs. late fusion layers) and training data size requirements, demonstrating that AdaptDraft recovers 85%+ of full-retraining speedup gains with <10% of the compute cost.

title: EAGLE-3 for Multimodal LLMs: Extending Training-Time Test to Vision-Language Speculative Decoding
description: Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 have demonstrated impressive speedups for text-only LLMs, but vision-language models (VLMs) such as LLaVA, InternVL, and Qwen-VL remain underexplored in this space. VLMs face unique challenges: the draft model must handle heterogeneous feature streams (visual tokens from a vision encoder plus text token embeddings), and the cross-modal attention patterns make naive feature reuse from top layers less reliable. Proposed Method: We adapt EAGLE-3's training-time test and multi-layer feature fusion paradigm to VLMs. Specifically, we design a multimodal draft model that fuses features from multiple transformer layers of the LLM backbone alongside projected visual features at multiple resolutions. During training-time test, we expose the draft model to diverse visual-text interleaving scenarios, enabling it to learn robust cross-modal continuation. We introduce a visual context gating mechanism that dynamically weights visual versus textual feature contributions during draft token generation. Experiments: We evaluate on (1) image captioning (COCO, NoCaps), (2) visual question answering (VQAv2, MMBench), (3) document understanding (DocVQA), and (4) multi-image reasoning tasks. Metrics include speedup ratio, acceptance rate, and output quality. We compare against vanilla speculative decoding and EAGLE-2 adapted for VLMs across Qwen2-VL-7B and InternVL2-8B.

title: Adaptive Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding via Query Complexity Routing
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 uses a single fixed draft model regardless of input complexity. Simple queries (factual lookups, short completions) likely need fewer draft tokens and smaller draft models, while complex reasoning chains demand larger, more capable drafters. A one-size-fits-all approach wastes compute on simple queries or degrades acceptance rates on hard ones.

Proposed Method: We introduce a lightweight query complexity router that, given the input prompt and current context, predicts (1) optimal draft depth (number of draft tokens per step) and (2) selects among a pool of draft models of varying sizes trained with EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion. The router is a small MLP operating on compressed hidden states from the target model's early layers, trained via reinforcement learning where the reward signal is empirical tokens-accepted-per-second on a held-out calibration set. During inference, the router adds negligible overhead (~0.1ms) but dynamically configures the speculative decoding pipeline.

Experiments: (1) Build a pool of 3 EAGLE-3 draft models (68M, 200M, 500M parameters) for Llama-3.1-70B. (2) Evaluate on MT-Bench, GSM8K, HumanEval, and long-form generation. (3) Compare throughput and speedup ratios vs. static EAGLE-3 across batch sizes 1–64. (4) Analyze router decisions vs. query complexity metrics. Expected outcome: 15-25% additional throughput gains on mixed-complexity workloads.

title: SpecDraft-Adaptive: Online Difficulty-Aware Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Inference
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 and similar speculative decoding methods use a single fixed draft model regardless of input complexity. Easy prompts (factual Q&A) and hard prompts (multi-step reasoning) have vastly different token predictability, meaning a single draft model either wastes capacity on easy inputs or underperforms on hard ones. This mismatch limits overall throughput gains in production serving systems handling diverse workloads.

Proposed Method: We introduce SpecDraft-Adaptive, a lightweight online routing mechanism that dynamically selects among a pool of draft models (e.g., small/medium EAGLE-3 variants with different training data scales) based on real-time difficulty signals. We derive difficulty proxies from: (1) draft model token acceptance rates over a short sliding window, (2) target model top-layer feature entropy, and (3) prompt perplexity estimates. A bandit-style controller (contextual Thompson Sampling) learns per-request routing policies that maximize tokens-per-second subject to latency constraints. The draft pool is trained jointly using distillation from EAGLE-3's multi-layer fusion paradigm.

Experiments: We evaluate on MT-Bench, HumanEval, MATH, and long-context summarization under simulated production request mixtures. Baselines include EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3 (fixed), and SpecInfer. Metrics: wall-clock speedup, acceptance rate distribution, and throughput at batch sizes 1/16/64. We hypothesize 10-20% additional throughput gains over EAGLE-3 on heterogeneous workloads.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Online Draft Model Fine-Tuning for Personalized Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 and similar speculative decoding methods train a single universal draft model, but individual users exhibit highly consistent stylistic and domain-specific patterns (e.g., a coder always writing Python, a researcher querying scientific text). A static draft model cannot exploit these patterns, leaving acceptance rates suboptimal for specialized users.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight online adaptation framework where the EAGLE-3 draft model is continuously fine-tuned on a per-user interaction history using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). After each conversation turn, accepted draft tokens (which represent high-quality target model outputs) are used as supervised signal to update a small LoRA adapter on the draft model. To avoid catastrophic forgetting and maintain generality, we employ elastic weight consolidation (EWC) regularization anchored to the base EAGLE-3 weights. The adapter update occurs asynchronously during idle prefill phases to avoid latency overhead.

Experiments: (1) Simulate user-specialized sessions across coding, math reasoning, medical, and creative writing domains using existing benchmarks. (2) Measure token acceptance rate and wall-clock speedup versus static EAGLE-3 as a function of interaction turns. (3) Evaluate catastrophic forgetting on held-out general tasks. (4) Ablate LoRA rank, EWC strength, and update frequency. We expect 10-20% acceptance rate improvements for domain-specialized sessions within 50 turns.

title: SpecFusion: Heterogeneous Draft Ensembles for Speculative Decoding via Confidence-Weighted Token Selection
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 rely on a single draft model, which may specialize well for certain token distributions (e.g., code, reasoning chains, conversational text) but underperform on others. A single draft model cannot simultaneously optimize acceptance rates across diverse generation contexts, leaving speedup potential on the table.

Proposed Method: We propose SpecFusion, a framework that maintains a small pool of lightweight heterogeneous draft models (e.g., one fine-tuned on code, one on reasoning traces, one on general chat) built on top of EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion backbone. At each draft step, a lightweight router—trained via online distillation using acceptance rate as the reward signal—selects or interpolates token distributions from the pool based on current context features. We introduce a confidence-weighted draft selection mechanism that uses the target model's top-layer activations to dynamically pick the most promising draft without additional forward passes.

Experiments: (1) Acceptance rate and speedup across domain-specific benchmarks (HumanEval, MATH, MT-Bench, long-document QA). (2) Ablation over pool size (1–4 drafts) and routing strategies. (3) Overhead analysis of router inference cost vs. acceptance rate gains. (4) Comparison against EAGLE-3 single-draft and Medusa baselines. We target demonstrating 10–20% additional speedup over EAGLE-3 on mixed-domain workloads.

title: AdaptiDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection via Complexity-Aware Routing for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding systems like EAGLE-3 use a single fixed draft model regardless of input complexity. Simple queries waste capacity of powerful draft models, while complex reasoning tasks may exceed their capability, reducing acceptance rates and overall speedup. A routing mechanism that dynamically selects among multiple draft models of varying capacities could maximize throughput across diverse workloads.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight complexity classifier (a small MLP head attached to early target model layers) that predicts input difficulty from the first forward pass, routing each request to one of three draft models: a tiny 1-layer draft for simple completions, a standard EAGLE-3 draft for moderate tasks, and a larger capacity draft augmented with chain-of-thought auxiliary training for complex reasoning. The classifier is trained jointly with the draft models using a differentiable routing loss that balances acceptance rate against draft computational cost. We further introduce a dynamic batch-level scheduler that groups requests by predicted complexity to maximize GPU utilization.

Experiments: We evaluate on diverse benchmarks spanning coding (HumanEval), math reasoning (MATH-500), chitchat (MT-Bench), and long-document QA (LongBench). Metrics include acceptance rate per tier, wall-clock speedup, and throughput at batch sizes 1-128. Ablations compare single-model baselines, fixed-threshold routing, and learned routing. Target models: Llama-3.1-70B and DeepSeek-R1-32B.

title: AdaptDraft: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for Speculative Decoding via Lightweight Fine-Tuning of EAGLE-3
description: Problem: While EAGLE-3 achieves strong general-purpose speedups, speculative decoding performance degrades when the target LLM is fine-tuned or deployed in specialized domains (medical, legal, code), because the draft model's token prediction distribution diverges from the adapted target model. Retraining the full draft model for each domain-specific variant is prohibitively expensive. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptDraft, a parameter-efficient adaptation framework for EAGLE-3-style draft models. Given a domain-specific target model (e.g., a LoRA-fine-tuned medical LLM), we train a small LoRA adapter on top of the frozen EAGLE-3 draft model using only domain-specific data and the training-time test objective from EAGLE-3. The multi-layer feature fusion architecture of EAGLE-3 naturally exposes intermediate representations that can be selectively adapted. We further propose a draft-target alignment loss that minimizes token-level KL divergence between draft and target distributions on unlabeled domain text, requiring no human annotations. Experiments: We evaluate on four domain-adapted LLaMA-3 variants (medical, legal, code, math) and measure speculative decoding acceptance rates, wall-clock speedup ratios, and adapter training cost. We compare against full draft retraining, no adaptation, and vanilla LoRA fine-tuning baselines, demonstrating that AdaptDraft recovers 85%+ of optimal speedup with <2% of retraining compute.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for EAGLE-3 via Lightweight Fine-Tuning with Synthetic Speculative Data
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a universal draft model that accelerates general LLMs, but acceptance rates degrade significantly when the target model is fine-tuned for specialized domains (medical, legal, code-heavy reasoning) where token distributions shift substantially from pretraining data. A single static draft model cannot optimally track domain-specific target model behavior, leaving substantial speedup potential untapped. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a framework that rapidly adapts EAGLE-3 draft models to specialized target models using synthetic speculative data. Given a domain-specialized target LLM, we (1) generate domain-specific training sequences by sampling the target model on small seed corpora, (2) extract multi-layer feature trajectories using EAGLE-3's training-time test mechanism, and (3) fine-tune the draft model with a combined token-prediction and feature-alignment loss using LoRA, requiring only ~50K tokens of domain data. We additionally propose a 'draft drift' metric to quantify distribution shift between general and domain-specific draft models, enabling automated triggers for re-adaptation. Experiments: We evaluate on four specialized domains (medical QA, legal reasoning, competitive coding, mathematical proofs) using Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 base models fine-tuned per domain. We measure speedup ratio, token acceptance rate, and adaptation compute cost, comparing against vanilla EAGLE-3 and full retraining baselines.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Speculative Decoding with Dynamic Draft Model Selection via Reinforcement Learning
description: Problem: Current speculative decoding systems like EAGLE-3 use a fixed draft model regardless of the input context, task type, or reasoning complexity. However, different queries (e.g., simple factual lookups vs. multi-step reasoning chains) may benefit from draft models of varying capacity and architecture. A small, fast draft model may suffice for simple queries but underperform on complex reasoning tasks, while a larger draft wastes compute on trivial inputs. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight routing controller trained via reinforcement learning that dynamically selects among a pool of draft models (varying in size and architecture, including EAGLE-3 style token-prediction drafts and shallower n-gram models) based on a featurized representation of the incoming query and recent acceptance rate history. The RL reward signal combines token acceptance rate and wall-clock latency, encouraging the router to maximize throughput across diverse workloads. We also propose a progressive draft switching mechanism that can change draft models mid-sequence when acceptance rates drop. Experiments: We evaluate on chat benchmarks (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval), reasoning tasks (MATH, GSM8K), and long-context retrieval tasks using LLaMA-3 and Qwen-2.5 base models. We compare against fixed-draft EAGLE-3 baselines and measure speedup ratios, acceptance rates, and throughput at varying batch sizes.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Domain-Aware Draft Model Specialization for EAGLE-3 via Mixture-of-Experts Token Prediction
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single monolithic draft model that must serve across diverse domains (code, math reasoning, general chat, medical text), yet draft acceptance rates vary significantly across domains. A universal draft model may underfit domain-specific token distributions, leaving substantial speedup potential unrealized. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, which replaces EAGLE-3's single draft head with a lightweight Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) token prediction head. Each expert specializes in a domain, with a low-overhead router conditioned on EAGLE-3's multi-layer fused features selecting the top-2 experts per draft step. Crucially, we apply training-time test (EAGLE-3's technique) per expert, exposing each expert to domain-specific feature distributions during training. At inference, the router adds negligible latency (<1ms) while the selected experts produce domain-calibrated draft tokens. We also propose a continual domain adaptation protocol: new domain experts can be fine-tuned without retraining the base draft model. Experiments: We evaluate on LLaMA-3.1-70B and Qwen2.5-72B across five domains (HumanEval, MATH, MT-Bench, MedQA, LegalBench), measuring speculative acceptance rate τ, wall-clock speedup, and throughput at batch sizes 1/16/64. We compare against EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3, and domain-specific EAGLE-3 fine-tunes, expecting 10-20% additional speedup in specialized domains with minimal regression elsewhere.

title: AdaptDraft: Domain-Adaptive Speculative Decoding via Lightweight Draft Model Fine-Tuning with Multi-Layer Feature Fusion
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 demonstrates that multi-layer feature fusion and direct token prediction enable strong speculative decoding speedups on general chat and reasoning tasks. However, when LLMs are fine-tuned for specialized domains (e.g., medical, legal, code generation), the distribution shift between the base model and the specialized target model degrades draft acceptance rates, nullifying speedup gains. A single general-purpose draft model cannot efficiently serve a fleet of domain-adapted target models. Proposed Method: We propose AdaptDraft, a parameter-efficient adaptation framework for EAGLE-3-style draft models. Given a domain-fine-tuned target LLM, we freeze the EAGLE-3 draft backbone and train only small LoRA adapters inserted into the multi-layer feature fusion module. We introduce a 'draft consistency loss' that aligns the fused feature representations of the draft model to those of the domain-specific target at multiple layers simultaneously, bootstrapping adaptation with minimal data (~10K domain examples). Experiments: We evaluate on four specialized domains: medical QA (MedQA), legal reasoning (LegalBench), scientific literature (SciQ), and code (HumanEval). We measure token acceptance rate, end-to-end speedup, and adapter training cost versus full draft model retraining. Baselines include vanilla EAGLE-3 applied to fine-tuned targets and full draft model retraining. We demonstrate AdaptDraft recovers 90%+ of in-domain speedup with <5% of retraining compute.

title: Collaborative Speculative Decoding: Training Draft Models Across Heterogeneous LLM Families via Universal Feature Alignment
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 train dedicated draft models per target LLM, requiring expensive retraining whenever the target model changes or is updated. This creates significant overhead in production environments hosting multiple LLM variants.

Proposed Method: We propose UniDraft, a single universal draft model that serves multiple heterogeneous target LLMs simultaneously. Building on EAGLE-3's training-time test and multi-layer feature fusion, we introduce a cross-model feature alignment module that learns a shared latent space across different LLM families (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, etc.). During training, we apply contrastive alignment losses that map heterogeneous top-layer features from different target models into a unified representation, enabling one draft model to predict tokens for any registered target model. At inference, the draft model receives a lightweight model-identity embedding alongside fused features to condition generation appropriately per target.

Experiments: (1) Single-model speedup comparison against per-model EAGLE-3 baselines across Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, and Mistral families; (2) Zero-shot transfer to unseen LLMs not in training; (3) Multi-tenant serving throughput at batch sizes 16-128 with mixed target-model requests; (4) Ablations on alignment loss design and number of supported target models (2, 4, 8). We evaluate on MT-Bench, HumanEval, and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

title: EAGLE-3 for Multimodal LLMs: Speculative Decoding with Cross-Modal Feature Fusion
description:
Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 have been developed exclusively for text-only LLMs, leaving vision-language models (VLMs) such as LLaVA and Qwen-VL without effective inference acceleration. VLMs are particularly costly because visual tokens dramatically lengthen context, yet existing draft models cannot exploit the rich visual feature representations embedded in target model layers.

Proposed Method: We extend EAGLE-3's training-time test paradigm to multimodal settings by designing a draft model that performs direct token prediction while fusing multi-layer features from both the language backbone and the vision encoder. Specifically, we introduce a lightweight cross-modal attention module in the draft model that attends to frozen visual patch embeddings alongside multi-layer text features during training-time test, enabling the draft model to condition token proposals on visual context without increasing inference latency. We also construct a multimodal speculative training corpus pairing diverse image-text conversations with reasoning traces.

Experiments: We evaluate on LLaVA-1.6, InternVL2, and Qwen2-VL across five benchmarks: visual QA (VQAv2, MMBench), image captioning (COCO), multimodal reasoning (MathVista), and OCR (DocVQA). Metrics include speedup ratio, acceptance rate, and output quality (CIDEr, accuracy). We ablate cross-modal fusion depth and compare against vanilla EAGLE-3 adapted naively to VLMs.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Context-Aware Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding Across Diverse Query Distributions
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for average-case performance across all query types. However, LLM deployments face highly heterogeneous query distributions—coding, math reasoning, creative writing, and dialogue have vastly different token prediction patterns. A single draft model may achieve high acceptance rates on some tasks while performing poorly on others, leaving speedup potential untapped.

Proposed Method: We train a small pool of lightweight, task-specialized draft models (e.g., 4-6 models) using EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion and direct token prediction framework. We introduce a query router—a tiny classifier operating on the first few tokens and early target model features—that dynamically selects the most suitable draft model at inference time. The router is trained jointly using draft acceptance rate as a differentiable reward signal via REINFORCE, avoiding costly oracle labeling. We also explore soft mixture-of-drafts where multiple draft models contribute weighted token probability distributions.

Experiments: (1) Compare single vs. specialized draft models on MT-Bench, HumanEval, MATH, and long-form generation; (2) Measure routing latency overhead vs. speedup gains; (3) Evaluate on mixed-distribution production-like traffic; (4) Ablate router architectures (linear probe vs. small MLP vs. attention-based); (5) Compare soft-mixture vs. hard-selection routing strategies across batch sizes in SGLang.

title: AdaptEAGLE: Domain-Adaptive Draft Models for Speculative Decoding via Continual Training-Time Test
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3's draft model is trained on general-purpose data, leading to suboptimal acceptance rates when deployed on domain-specific LLMs (e.g., medical, legal, code-specialized models) where token distributions diverge significantly from general corpora. Retraining draft models from scratch for each specialized target model is computationally prohibitive.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptEAGLE, which leverages EAGLE-3's training-time test (TTT) framework for continual domain adaptation of draft models. Given a specialized target model, we perform lightweight TTT fine-tuning of the draft model using a small domain-specific corpus (1-10M tokens), dynamically fusing multi-layer features from the specialized target model during adaptation. We introduce a domain-shift regularizer that prevents catastrophic forgetting of general capabilities while rapidly adapting to domain-specific token distributions. Additionally, we propose a data-efficient active sampling strategy that selects the most informative domain samples based on draft model uncertainty.

Experiments: We evaluate on four domain-specialized LLMs (medical: BioMistral, legal: LegalBERT-LLM, code: DeepSeek-Coder, math: Qwen-Math) using domain benchmarks. We measure speedup ratios, acceptance rates, and adaptation cost (GPU-hours) compared to full retraining and vanilla EAGLE-3. We target demonstrating 90% of full-retraining speedup at under 5% of its computational cost.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Confidence-Guided Dynamic Draft Length Selection for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed or heuristically-determined draft length (number of tokens proposed per step), which is suboptimal because different decoding contexts have varying predictability. Easy, repetitive, or formulaic sequences could benefit from longer drafts, while ambiguous or creative generation warrants shorter ones. Uniform draft lengths waste computation on hard-to-predict tokens and leave efficiency gains unrealized on easy sequences.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, which trains a lightweight meta-predictor on top of EAGLE-3's draft model to estimate the expected acceptance rate for the next K tokens given the current hidden state and recent acceptance history. At inference time, the meta-predictor outputs an optimal draft length (e.g., 3–10 tokens) dynamically per decoding step. We train the meta-predictor using a replay buffer of (context, draft_length, realized_acceptance_rate) tuples collected during EAGLE-3 inference, optimizing for expected token throughput rather than raw acceptance rate.

Experiments: (1) Measure speedup ratio vs. fixed-length EAGLE-3 across tasks: code generation, math reasoning, open-ended chat, summarization; (2) Analyze draft length distributions per task type; (3) Ablate meta-predictor architectures (MLP vs. small transformer); (4) Evaluate batched inference throughput at varying batch sizes in SGLang; (5) Measure overhead of meta-predictor to ensure net positive throughput gains.

title: EAGLE-3 for Multimodal LLMs: Speculative Decoding with Cross-Modal Feature Fusion
description:
Problem: Speculative decoding accelerations like EAGLE-3 have been developed for text-only LLMs, but large vision-language models (VLMs) such as LLaVA and Qwen-VL face even greater inference bottlenecks due to long visual token sequences combined with autoregressive text generation. Extending draft-model-based speculative sampling to VLMs is non-trivial because visual features from the vision encoder introduce a new modality that the draft model must condition on.

Proposed Method: We propose MM-EAGLE, a speculative decoding framework for VLMs that extends EAGLE-3's training-time test and multi-layer feature fusion to the multimodal setting. The draft model fuses multi-layer text features (as in EAGLE-3) with compressed cross-modal visual context vectors extracted from intermediate vision-language attention layers. During training-time test, the draft model sees both linguistic and visual feature distributions, enabling it to predict tokens conditioned on visual grounding. We introduce a lightweight cross-modal attention adapter in the draft model to efficiently incorporate visual signals without significantly increasing draft model size.

Experiments: We evaluate MM-EAGLE on VLMs (LLaVA-1.6-7B/13B, Qwen2-VL-7B) across tasks including image captioning (COCO), visual QA (MMBench, MMMU), and document understanding (DocVQA). Metrics include wall-clock speedup, acceptance rate, and output quality. We compare against text-only EAGLE-3, vanilla speculative sampling, and Medusa baselines adapted for VLMs.

title: AdaptDraft: Online Distillation of User-Adaptive Draft Models for Personalized Speculative Decoding
description: Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single universal draft model, but real-world LLM deployments serve heterogeneous users with highly distinct query distributions (code, math, creative writing, etc.). A universal draft model wastes capacity on irrelevant token distributions, leaving per-user acceptance rates suboptimal. We propose AdaptDraft, a lightweight framework that continuously fine-tunes small user-specific draft model adapters (LoRA modules) using EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion and training-time test paradigm, but driven by online feedback collected during actual serving. Method: For each user session, accepted/rejected tokens from speculative decoding episodes form a self-supervised signal. We maintain a shared frozen EAGLE-3 draft backbone and attach cheap LoRA adapters per user cluster (clustered by query embedding similarity). The adapters are updated via async gradient steps between inference calls using accepted token sequences as ground truth, distilling the target model's implicit distribution into the adapter. This preserves EAGLE-3's direct token prediction and multi-layer fusion benefits while personalizing draft distributions. Experiments: (1) Simulated personalized workloads from ShareGPT/HumanEval/MATH with user-stratified splits; (2) acceptance rate and wall-clock speedup vs. universal EAGLE-3 and vanilla LoRA fine-tuning; (3) adapter storage and update latency analysis; (4) ablation on cluster granularity and update frequency across Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 families.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Serving via Workload-Aware Routing
description: Problem: In production LLM serving, requests exhibit highly heterogeneous complexity—coding tasks, multi-step reasoning, and simple Q&A have vastly different acceptance rate profiles for speculative decoding draft models. A single draft model (e.g., EAGLE-3) optimized on aggregate data may underperform for specific workload distributions, wasting draft tokens and reducing throughput gains. Proposed Method: We train a lightweight router that predicts, from the prompt embedding and early decoding statistics, which draft model from a small pool (e.g., EAGLE-3 variants fine-tuned on domain-specific data: code, math reasoning, conversational) will achieve the highest token acceptance rate for the current request. The router uses a multi-armed bandit formulation with online updates, adapting to shifting workload distributions in real-time. Each draft model is trained using EAGLE-3's training-time test paradigm but with domain-curated corpora. The router adds <1ms overhead and selects the draft model per request or per decoding chunk. Experiments: (1) Single-domain accuracy—measure per-domain speedup vs. a universal EAGLE-3 baseline on code (HumanEval), math (MATH-500), and chat benchmarks; (2) Mixed-workload serving simulation with varying traffic ratios; (3) Online adaptation experiments with distribution shifts; (4) Ablation on router architectures and update frequencies. We target >15% additional throughput over vanilla EAGLE-3 on mixed workloads.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding Across Heterogeneous Query Distributions
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for a fixed data distribution, but real-world LLM deployments face heterogeneous query distributions (code, math reasoning, chat, long-form generation) where a single draft model cannot simultaneously maximize acceptance rates across all domains. Routing each query to a specialized draft model could significantly improve token acceptance rates and overall throughput.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight router (small MLP operating on the first few tokens of the query + target model's top-layer embedding) that selects among K domain-specialized EAGLE-3 draft models at inference time. Each draft model is trained on domain-specific data using EAGLE-3's training-time test framework and multi-layer feature fusion. The router is trained jointly with a mixture-of-experts distillation objective that maximizes expected acceptance length across all domains. We also explore a soft-routing variant that blends draft logits from multiple models weighted by router confidence.

Experiments: (1) Train K=4 specialized draft models (code, math, chat, general) on domain partitions of the EAGLE-3 training corpus; (2) Evaluate on mixed-domain benchmarks (HumanEval, MATH, MT-Bench, summarization) measuring per-domain and aggregate speedup ratios; (3) Compare against a single large EAGLE-3 draft model with equivalent total parameter budget; (4) Ablate router architectures and soft vs. hard routing under varying batch compositions in SGLang.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Input-Complexity-Aware Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Current speculative decoding systems like EAGLE-3 use a fixed draft model regardless of input complexity. Simple queries (factual lookups, short completions) could be served by a smaller, faster draft model, while complex reasoning chains require a more capable draft model. This mismatch wastes compute on easy inputs and potentially limits acceptance rates on hard inputs.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight router (a small MLP operating on the first few target model layers' features) that predicts, at inference time, which of several draft models (varying in capacity: e.g., 1-layer, 2-layer, 4-layer EAGLE-3 style drafters) will yield the highest expected tokens-accepted-per-second for the current input. The router is trained via reinforcement learning using actual measured acceptance rates across a diverse corpus. We additionally introduce a dynamic switching mechanism that re-evaluates draft model selection every K speculative steps based on running acceptance rate statistics.

Experiments: (1) Train router on Llama-3.1-8B and 70B with three draft model tiers; (2) Evaluate on MT-Bench, HumanEval, MATH, and long-document summarization; (3) Compare wall-clock speedup vs. EAGLE-3 fixed drafting; (4) Ablate router architecture and switching frequency; (5) Measure router overhead vs. throughput gains across batch sizes 1-64 in SGLang.

title: SpecFusion: Combining Multiple Draft Models via Mixture-of-Experts for Adaptive Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: Different query types (coding, math reasoning, open-ended chat) have vastly different token distribution patterns, yet current speculative decoding systems like EAGLE-3 use a single draft model regardless of input context. This leads to suboptimal acceptance rates across diverse workloads.

Proposed Method: We propose SpecFusion, a mixture-of-experts draft architecture where specialized lightweight draft models (trained on domain-specific data) are dynamically selected per-generation based on a fast router that analyzes the input prompt embedding. Building on EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion and direct token prediction, each expert draft model uses the same training-time test technique but is fine-tuned on distinct data distributions (code, mathematics, conversation). A learned gating network selects the top-k experts per step, combining their draft token distributions via weighted averaging before speculative verification by the target LLM.

Experiments: (1) Train 3-5 expert draft models using EAGLE-3's methodology on domain-specific corpora. (2) Evaluate acceptance rates and speedup ratios per domain against EAGLE-3 single-model baseline on HumanEval, MATH, MT-Bench, and ShareGPT. (3) Measure routing overhead vs. acceptance rate gain trade-offs. (4) Test on mixed-domain batches at batch sizes 1-64 in SGLang. We hypothesize 10-20% acceptance rate improvement on specialized tasks with minimal routing overhead.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding Across Heterogeneous Query Distributions
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 trains a single draft model optimized for a fixed training distribution, but real-world LLM deployments face heterogeneous query types (coding, math reasoning, casual chat, long-form generation) with wildly different token predictability profiles. A single draft model may achieve high acceptance rates on some query types while performing poorly on others, leaving significant speedup potential untapped.

Proposed Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight meta-routing system that maintains a small bank of specialized EAGLE-3 draft models (e.g., one per domain: code, math, chat) alongside a query classifier trained to predict draft acceptance rates before generation begins. At inference time, the classifier selects the best draft model in ~1ms using a compressed query embedding. Additionally, we introduce an online adaptation mechanism: if mid-generation acceptance rates drop below a threshold, the system switches draft models without restarting generation. The classifier is trained using acceptance rate traces collected from existing EAGLE-3 runs as supervision signal.

Experiments: (1) Measure per-domain speedup ratios on MT-Bench, HumanEval, MATH, and long-document summarization. (2) Ablate static vs. adaptive selection vs. mid-generation switching. (3) Evaluate overhead of routing classifier vs. gained speedup. (4) Test on both Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 target models. Expected outcome: 15-25% additional speedup over single-model EAGLE-3 on mixed-distribution workloads.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Input-Complexity-Aware Dynamic Draft Length Scheduling for Speculative Decoding
description: Problem: Speculative decoding methods like EAGLE-3 use a fixed draft length (number of tokens proposed per step) regardless of input complexity. Easy prompts with predictable continuations could benefit from longer drafts, while complex or ambiguous inputs waste cycles on low-acceptance speculative tokens. This mismatch limits throughput gains in practice. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight scheduler that dynamically adjusts draft length at inference time based on predicted acceptance rates. Specifically, we train a small meta-predictor (a shallow MLP) that takes as input recent token acceptance history, entropy of the draft model's token distribution, and compressed representations of the last few target-model hidden states to predict the optimal draft budget for the next speculation step. The meta-predictor is trained via a small online reinforcement learning signal: reward is defined as tokens accepted per wall-clock second. We integrate AdaptiveDraft on top of EAGLE-3's direct token prediction and multi-layer fusion backbone. Experiments: We evaluate on diverse benchmarks (MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, long-form summarization, chain-of-thought reasoning) using Llama-3 and Qwen-2.5 families. Metrics include speedup ratio, acceptance rate variance, and throughput across batch sizes 1–64. Ablations compare fixed vs. adaptive scheduling and examine the meta-predictor's overhead. We expect 10–20% additional throughput improvement over EAGLE-3 baselines on mixed-complexity workloads.

title: AdaptDraft: Input-Adaptive Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous Speculative Decoding
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 and similar speculative decoding methods train a single draft model optimized for average-case performance across all inputs. However, LLM queries exhibit significant heterogeneity—coding tasks, mathematical reasoning, and conversational responses have vastly different token predictability and acceptance rate profiles. A one-size-fits-all draft model leaves substantial speedup gains on the table for specialized query types.

Proposed Method: We train a small family of lightweight, specialized draft models (e.g., one per domain: code, math, chat, instruction-following) using EAGLE-3's training-time test framework with domain-specific corpora. At inference time, a ultra-lightweight router (a 2-layer MLP operating on the first few tokens' embeddings or a prompt prefix classifier) selects which draft model to deploy without adding meaningful latency. We additionally explore mixture-of-draft approaches where multiple draft models contribute candidates that are jointly evaluated in a single verification pass.

Experiments: (1) Train domain-specialized EAGLE-3 draft models on HumanEval/MBPP (code), MATH/GSM8K (math), ShareGPT (chat); (2) benchmark acceptance rates and wall-clock speedup per domain vs. a single universal draft model; (3) evaluate router overhead and accuracy on mixed workloads; (4) test throughput at batch sizes 1–128 in SGLang across Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1 targets; (5) ablate routing strategies including confidence-based dynamic switching mid-sequence.

title: AdaptiDraft: Input-Adaptive Draft Model Selection for Speculative Decoding via Complexity-Aware Routing
description:
Problem: EAGLE-3 achieves impressive speedups with a fixed draft model architecture, but different inputs vary dramatically in predictability — simple factual queries may be well-served by a tiny draft model while complex multi-step reasoning benefits from a larger one. Using a single draft model for all inputs leaves significant efficiency gains untapped.

Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptiDraft, a complexity-aware routing framework that dynamically selects among a pool of draft models of varying sizes (e.g., 1-layer, 3-layer, 6-layer EAGLE-3-style heads) based on input characteristics. A lightweight router (a small MLP operating on the first few target model hidden states) predicts input 'speculative difficulty' — estimated acceptance rate — and routes to the appropriate draft model. The router is trained jointly with the draft pool using a differentiable surrogate for expected wall-clock speedup, combining acceptance rate prediction with FLOPs cost penalties. We also introduce a dynamic switching mechanism that can upgrade/downgrade the draft model mid-sequence if early tokens reveal mispredicted difficulty.

Experiments: (1) Speedup benchmarks across MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and long-form generation on Llama-3 and DeepSeek-R1; (2) Ablations on router size and pool configurations; (3) Analysis of routing decisions across task categories; (4) Throughput scaling at batch sizes 1–128 in SGLang, comparing against fixed EAGLE-3 baselines.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection for Heterogeneous LLM Serving via Workload-Aware Speculative Sampling
description:
Problem: Production LLM serving systems handle highly diverse workloads—coding queries, math reasoning, casual chat, retrieval-augmented generation—each with distinct token distributions and acceptance rate profiles. A single static draft model (as in EAGLE-3) may be suboptimal across this heterogeneity: reasoning tasks benefit from deeper feature fusion while conversational tasks may need lighter, faster drafts. No existing work dynamically selects or blends draft strategies at inference time based on input characteristics.

Proposed Method: We train a lightweight router (a small MLP or attention head over the first few target-model layers) that, given an incoming prompt, selects among a bank of specialized EAGLE-3-style draft models (e.g., one fine-tuned on code corpora, one on reasoning chains, one on dialogue). The router is trained end-to-end using a differentiable surrogate of acceptance rate as the reward signal. At serving time, the router adds <1ms overhead and dispatches to the appropriate draft model. We additionally explore soft mixing—weighted ensemble of two draft models' token distributions—for ambiguous inputs.

Experiments: (1) Acceptance rate and wall-clock speedup on domain-specific benchmarks (HumanEval, MATH, MT-Bench, RAG-QA); (2) Mixed-workload serving simulation showing throughput vs. latency tradeoffs versus single-draft baselines; (3) Ablation on router capacity and number of specialist drafts; (4) Comparison against EAGLE-3 with a single large draft model of equivalent total parameter count.

title: AdaptDraft: Dynamically Adjusting Draft Model Depth During Speculative Decoding via Learned Query Routing
description: Problem: EAGLE-3's multi-layer feature fusion uses a fixed fusion strategy across all inputs, yet different token predictions vary widely in difficulty — simple continuations need only shallow features while complex reasoning steps benefit from richer multi-layer representations. Static fusion wastes computation on easy tokens and may under-utilize available context for hard ones. Proposed Method: We introduce AdaptDraft, a speculative decoding framework that learns a lightweight routing module (a small MLP trained jointly with the draft model) to dynamically select which subset of target model layers to fuse for each draft step. The router outputs a discrete selection over predefined layer-combination presets (e.g., shallow-only, mid-only, full fusion), controlled via a differentiable Gumbel-softmax during training. Training uses the training-time test paradigm from EAGLE-3, but augments the loss with an efficiency regularizer penalizing average fusion depth, encouraging the router to prefer cheaper combinations when sufficient. Experiments: We evaluate on Llama-3 (8B, 70B) and DeepSeek-R1 across MT-Bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and long-form generation. Metrics include token acceptance rate, wall-clock speedup, and average fusion depth per task type. We analyze routing decisions qualitatively to validate that harder tokens trigger deeper fusion, and benchmark against EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3, and Medusa baselines.

title: AdaptiveDraft: Dynamic Draft Model Selection and Blending for Heterogeneous Inference Workloads
description: Problem: Real-world LLM deployments face highly heterogeneous query distributions—coding, reasoning, chat, summarization—each with distinct token distribution characteristics. A single draft model (even EAGLE-3) trained on mixed data may underperform specialized drafts on specific task types, yet maintaining multiple draft models per target LLM is memory-prohibitive. Method: We propose AdaptiveDraft, a lightweight router-based speculative decoding framework that maintains a small bank of low-rank delta adapters (LoRA) on top of a single EAGLE-3 draft backbone, one per task domain. At inference time, a 3-layer classifier observes the first 32 tokens of context and selects or interpolates adapter weights before drafting begins. We introduce 'draft blending'—soft merging of two adapter sets weighted by router confidence—to handle ambiguous inputs. Training follows EAGLE-3's training-time test paradigm but adds domain-balanced sampling with adapter-specific gradient routing. Experiments: (1) Speedup ratio across per-domain test sets (HumanEval, MATH, MT-Bench, CNN/DM, LegalBench) vs. EAGLE-3 single-model baseline; (2) Memory overhead vs. accuracy tradeoff as adapter rank varies; (3) Router latency impact on end-to-end throughput; (4) Ablation on blending vs. hard routing; (5) Generalization to new domains via rapid adapter fine-tuning with <1B tokens.
